teile.einleitung: Thyme is a small, fragrant herb found in many kitchens and gardens. It comes from the Mediterranean region and likes it sunny and dry. In Switzerland a wild relative also grows, wild thyme.
wichtigste: Common thyme comes from the Mediterranean region.
It has very small leaves and becomes woody with age.
Its flowers are mostly light purple to pink.
Thyme loves sunny, dry places.
The wild thyme in Switzerland is called “Quendel”.
Thyme tea is often drunk for coughs.

abschnitte.text: **Common thyme** is a low subshrub that grows about 10 to 40 centimetres tall. Its leaves are **very small**, narrow and often slightly rolled at the edge. Older stems become **woody**, and only the young shoots stay soft. In summer many small flowers appear, mostly **light purple to pink**. Thyme belongs to the **mint family**, like mint, sage and rosemary.

Common thyme originally grows on dry, stony slopes in the **Mediterranean region**. That is why in the garden, too, it likes a **sunny and dry** spot. Too much water and heavy, wet soil harm it. In Switzerland, **wild thyme** grows in the wild, also called creeping thyme. You find it on poor meadows, pastures and at the edges of paths, as high up as the Alps.

Thyme has a strong, spicy flavour. It goes well with **tomato sauce**, meat, potatoes and vegetables roasted in the oven. You can cook fresh sprigs along with the food and take them out later, or use dried leaves. There are many varieties, for example **lemon thyme**, which smells of lemon. Thyme is also part of the herb mixture “herbes de Provence”.

Thyme contains an **essential oil** with the substance **thymol**. This substance smells strong and stops bacteria from growing. That is why **thyme tea** has been drunk for a long time for **coughs** and colds. Pharmacies also sell cough syrup with thyme. For serious complaints, though, you should always see a doctor.

gewusst: The scent of thyme is held in tiny glandular hairs on the leaves.
Bees like to visit the flowers of thyme.

teile.einleitung: You find fir cones on every walk in the woods. The seeds of conifers lie between their scales. For squirrels and woodpeckers they are an important source of food.
wichtigste: The seeds lie between the scales of a cone.
When it rains the scales close, and in dry weather they open.
The seeds have a little wing and sail away on the wind.
Squirrels gnaw cones down to the core.
The great spotted woodpecker wedges cones into a woodpecker’s workshop.
Most conifers bear cones.

abschnitte.text: A cone consists of a central axis, the **spindle**, and many woody **scales**. The tree’s **seeds** lie between the scales. The cone protects them until they are ripe. Spruce, fir, pine, larch and Swiss stone pine all bear cones. Broadleaved trees, on the other hand, have other fruits such as nuts or berries.

Cones react to **moisture**. When it rains, the scales close so that the seeds stay dry. In dry weather they open again. This even works with cones that have been lying on the ground for a long time. Some people therefore use a cone as a simple **weather indicator**.

Many seeds in the cone have a thin **wing**. When they fall out, they spin and sail through the air. The **wind** carries them further away from the mother tree. That way new trees can grow in other places. Fresh cones are often sticky, because conifers produce **resin**, which protects the tree.

The **squirrel** bites off the scales to get at the seeds. What is left is a gnawed spindle with a few scales at the tip. The **great spotted woodpecker** wedges cones into a crack in the wood and hacks out the seeds. This workplace is called a **woodpecker’s workshop**. Underneath it you often find many shredded cones.

You can make bird food from cones. You press a mixture of **fat and seeds** between the scales. Then you hang the cone from a string in a tree. Tits and other birds like to peck at it in winter. Cones are also often used for Christmas decorations.

gewusst: The cones of the silver fir stand upright and fall apart while still on the tree, so most “fir cones” on the ground actually come from the spruce.
The cones of the Swiss stone pine do not open by themselves, and their seeds are spread mainly by the nutcracker.

teile.einleitung: An allotment garden is a small garden that you rent in a garden complex. In Switzerland these are mostly called family gardens. Here city dwellers grow vegetables, fruit and flowers.
wichtigste: The German name for the allotment garden, “Schrebergarten”, comes from the Leipzig doctor Moritz Schreber.
In Switzerland allotment gardens are mostly called family gardens.
A single piece of garden is called a plot.
Usually an association rents out the plots.
Many garden rules require you to plant part of the area.
In the Second World War, Switzerland grew far more food with the Battle for Crops.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, cities grew strongly. Many **working-class families** lived in cramped flats without greenery. A small garden offered fresh air, exercise and extra **vegetables**. The Leipzig doctor **Moritz Schreber** campaigned for exercise in the fresh air. After his death, playgrounds and gardens in Leipzig were named after him.

In Switzerland people mostly speak of **family gardens**. They are often rented out by **associations** on land belonging to the **municipality**. A complex is divided into many **plots**. Each plot is rented by one person or family. In many cities there are waiting lists, because the gardens are very popular.

Anyone who rents a plot must keep to the **garden rules**. Family gardens are meant for **growing** things and not only for leisure. That is why many associations require part of the area to be used for vegetables, fruit or flowers. On many plots there is a **garden shed**. It serves as shelter and as storage for tools. Living in it is usually not allowed.

In the **Second World War**, Switzerland was surrounded by countries at war. It wanted to grow as much of its own food as possible. This plan was called the **Anbauschlacht**, or Battle for Crops. After its originator, **Friedrich Traugott Wahlen**, it is also called the **Wahlen Plan**. Even on sports fields and in parks, potatoes and vegetables grew. In many family gardens and allotments in the cities, too, vegetables were grown at that time.

gewusst: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen later became a Federal Councillor.
Family gardens are important green islands for birds and insects in the city.

teile.einleitung: The scythe is an old tool for mowing grass and grain. Before there were machines, almost all meadows were mown by hand with the scythe. In the mountains it is still used today.
wichtigste: A scythe is a tool for mowing.
Its blade is long and curved.
The long wooden handle is called the snath.
You hold the scythe with both hands on two grips.
While mowing, you sharpen the blade with a whetstone.
Beating the blade thin with a hammer is called peening.
Today the scythe is used mainly on steep slopes and at edges.

abschnitte.text: A scythe consists of a **long, curved blade** and a long handle made of wood, the **snath**. On the snath sit **two grips**. The blade is fixed almost at a right angle at the lower end. In many Swiss dialects the scythe is called **“Sägesse”**.

You hold the scythe **with both hands on the grips** and swing it in a flat arc from right to left just above the ground. In doing so the grass is cut off and laid to the side. Good mowing takes practice. The power comes mainly from a turn of the upper body, not only from the arms. It is best to mow early in the morning, when the grass is still damp with dew.

A scythe must be very sharp. During the work you sharpen the blade again and again with a **whetstone**. You carry this in a small container filled with water at your belt so that it stays damp. From time to time the cutting edge also has to be **peened**. In this you beat it **thin** with a hammer on a small anvil. In this way it becomes fine and sharp again.

Today machines mostly do the mowing. The scythe is still used, however, where machines cannot go: on **steep slopes**, at the edges of paths, on stream banks and around trees. Especially in the Swiss **mountains**, some farming families still mow steep meadows by hand. Mowing with a scythe also spares insects and other small animals in the meadow.

Related to the scythe is the **sickle**. It has a **short, strongly curved blade** and only a small handle. You hold it in one hand and use it to cut smaller amounts of grass or grain. The sickle is even older than the scythe.

gewusst: In some regions there are scything competitions.
For a long time the scythe was the most important tool for the hay harvest, with which farmers collected fodder for the winter.

teile.einleitung: Hoverflies look like small wasps but are harmless flies. They can stay in one spot in the air and are important helpers in the garden.
wichtigste: Hoverflies belong to the flies and have two wings.
Many resemble wasps but can never sting.
The stripes protect them, because enemies take them for wasps.
They can stay in one spot in the air.
Adult hoverflies eat nectar and pollen.
The larvae of many species eat aphids.

abschnitte.text: Hoverflies belong to the **flies**. Like all flies, they have only **two wings**, while wasps and bees have four. Many hoverflies wear yellow and black stripes. You recognise them by their short antennae and the large eyes that cover almost the whole head. There are several thousand species worldwide.

Hoverflies have no sting and can **never sting**. Their stripes are a kind of camouflage. Birds and other enemies have learned that wasps sting, and avoid striped insects. The harmless hoverflies benefit from this. This imitation of a well-defended animal is called **mimicry**.

Hoverflies are excellent fliers. With very fast wing beats they can **hang in one spot in the air**, almost like a helicopter. That is where they get their name. In a flash they then shoot to the side or forwards. You often see them hovering over flowers.

Adult hoverflies feed on **nectar and pollen**. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower. In this way they help to pollinate plants, similar to bees. They especially like to visit open, flat flowers where they can easily reach the food.

The females often lay their eggs near colonies of aphids. The **larvae** of many species look like small maggots and eat **aphids**, one after another. A single larva can devour a great many aphids during its development. That is why hoverflies are popular with gardeners as **beneficial insects**.

gewusst: The larva of the drone fly, a kind of hoverfly, lives in muddy water and breathes through a long breathing tube. It is therefore called the rat-tailed maggot.
Some hoverflies migrate like migratory birds and fly south in large numbers over the Alpine passes in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The pea family is a large group of plants that includes pea, bean, clover and lentil. Their flowers recall a butterfly. With the help of bacteria, they can use nitrogen from the air.
wichtigste: A pea-family flower consists of a standard, wings and a keel.
Plants of the pea family form pods as fruits.
Nodule bacteria in the roots fix nitrogen from the air.
The peanut is botanically a legume.
Tofu is made from soya beans.
Laburnum is highly poisonous.

abschnitte.text: The flower of a **pea-family plant** has a special structure. At the top stands the large **standard**. At the sides lie two **wings**. Below, two fused petals form the **keel**. The stamens lie hidden inside it. When bees and bumblebees land, they press the keel down and so reach the pollen.

Plants of the pea family form a **pod** as their fruit. It develops from a single carpel and opens along two seams. That is why beans, peas and **lentils** are also called **pulses**. Lentils come in red, yellow, green and black varieties. Red lentils fall apart quickly when cooked and are often used for the Indian **dal**.

In the roots of many plants of the pea family live **nodule bacteria**. They fix **nitrogen** from the air and give it to the plant. In return they receive sugar. That is why **clover** and **lucerne** fertilise the soil in a natural way. **Red clover**, with its three-part leaves, is a protein-rich animal feed, also on Swiss meadows.

The **peanut** is not a true nut but a member of the pea family. After flowering, its fruit stalk grows into the ground, where the pods ripen. The **soya bean** is very rich in protein. Soya milk is made from soaked soya beans. If it is made to curdle and pressed, **tofu** is the result.

Not all plants of the pea family are edible. **Laburnum** is an ornamental shrub with long, hanging yellow flower clusters. All its parts, especially the seeds, contain the poison **cytisine**. Children should never put them in their mouths. The **black locust** from North America has feathered leaves and thorns. It was introduced as an ornamental tree and is regarded in Switzerland today as an **invasive neophyte**.

gewusst: The black locust is often called the false acacia.
Farmers sow clover to supply the soil with nitrogen without artificial fertiliser.

teile.einleitung: Butterflies are insects with large, often colourful wings that drink nectar from flowers with a long proboscis. Before they can fly, they live as a caterpillar and transform in a pupa. This transformation is one of the most exciting wonders of nature.
wichtigste: Butterflies are insects with six legs and four wings.
Their wings are covered with tiny scales.
They suck nectar from flowers with a coiled proboscis.
They go through a complete metamorphosis: egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult.
There are far more than 150,000 species, most of them moths.
Butterflies pollinate flowers and are food for many animals.
Many species are threatened in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Butterflies, also called **lepidopterans**, have six legs like all insects and a body made up of head, thorax and abdomen. Their four wings are covered with thousands of tiny **scales** that lie one over another like roof tiles. These scales produce the colours and patterns. On the head they have two antennae and a long **proboscis**, which they coil up like a garden hose.

The female lays her eggs on a suitable food plant. From them hatches a **caterpillar**, which does almost nothing but eat and moults several times. Then it transforms into a **pupa**, which in day-flying butterflies is often called a chrysalis. In the pupa the body is completely rebuilt until a finished butterfly hatches.

Adult butterflies mainly drink sweet **nectar** from flowers. Some also suck at rotting fruit, tree sap or damp ground to take in salts. Caterpillars, by contrast, eat leaves, and many species depend on one particular plant. The caterpillars of the peacock butterfly, for example, eat almost only stinging nettles.

Far more than 150,000 species of butterflies and moths are known worldwide. Most are **moths**, which are seen less often than the colourful day-flying butterflies. In Switzerland about 3,700 species live, of which about 200 are day-flying butterflies. Well-known examples are the brimstone, the swallowtail and the small tortoiseshell.

Butterflies **pollinate** flowers and are food for birds, bats and spiders. Unfortunately their numbers are falling because flower meadows are disappearing and poisons are being used. Almost half of the day-flying butterflies in Switzerland are on the **Red List** of threatened species. Anyone who has a natural garden with wild flowers and a few nettles is helping the butterflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a butterfly or moth.
The larva of the butterfly, which mainly eats and grows.
The resting stage in which the caterpillar rebuilds itself into a butterfly.
The complete transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.

gewusst: Butterflies taste with their feet.
The monarch butterfly migrates thousands of kilometres every year from Canada to Mexico.
In spring the painted lady flies from North Africa over the Alps as far as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The white willow is the largest native willow. It grows by rivers and streams and is also called the silver willow because of its silvery shining leaves. It has been important to people and animals for a long time.
wichtigste: The white willow is also called the silver willow because its leaves shine silvery.
It grows by rivers and streams.
It is the largest native willow.
It withstands flooding especially well.
Pollarded willows arise when the branches at the top of the trunk are cut off again and again.
In the past, willow bark was used against fever and pain.
In spring, willow flowers are an important first food for bees.

abschnitte.text: As the **largest native willow**, the white willow grows into a stately tree over 20 metres tall. Its leaves are long and narrow. Especially on the underside they are covered with fine, silky hairs. In the wind they therefore **shine silvery**. That is where its name comes from. The scientific name is Salix alba, and “alba” means white.

In the wild, the white willow grows **by rivers and streams**, in damp **floodplain forests** and on lake shores. It withstands **flooding** especially well and can stand in water for weeks. Its roots hold the bank firm. Broken-off twigs can even put down new roots in damp soil and become new trees.

In the past, the branches of many willows were cut off again and again at the top of the trunk. This created **pollarded willows** with a thick “head” from which new rods grow every year. From the **flexible willow rods**, **baskets**, fences and other objects were woven. In the hollows of old pollarded willows, birds such as the little owl often nest.

Willow bark was used long ago as a home remedy **against fever and pain**. It contains the substance **salicin**. From it, chemists later developed similar substances that are used as medicines. Well known is acetylsalicylic acid, the active ingredient of aspirin.

In spring, willows form fluffy flower clusters, the **catkins**. They bloom very early, when little else is blooming. For **bees**, bumblebees and other insects they are therefore an important **first food** with plenty of pollen and nectar. The seeds later bear white hairs and fly away with the wind.

gewusst: A cut willow twig that you stick in damp soil often simply takes root.
The name of the active substance salicin comes from the Latin name of the willow, Salix.

teile.einleitung: The Sihlwald in the canton of Zurich is one of the largest continuous beech forests on the Swiss Central Plateau. Since about 2000, no timber has been harvested there, so that the forest can develop back into wilderness.
wichtigste: The Sihlwald lies in the canton of Zurich in the Sihl valley.
It is shaped mainly by the common beech.
Since about 2000, the city of Zurich has given up harvesting timber.
In the west the Sihlwald is bounded by the range of hills of the Albis.
In the past the timber was floated down the Sihl to the city.
Together with the Langenberg Wildlife Park it forms the Wildnispark Zürich.
The Sihl Valley Railway has a station right at the Sihlwald.

abschnitte.text: The Sihlwald lies in the **canton of Zurich** in the valley of the Sihl, south of the city of Zurich. On the west side it is bounded by the range of hills of the **Albis**. The forest is shaped mainly by the **common beech**. For centuries it has belonged to the **city of Zurich**.

Over many centuries the Sihlwald supplied timber for Zurich, for building and for heating. The timber was **floated** down the **Sihl** to the city. That is, the trunks were left to drift down the river. Later roads and the railway were added. The **Sihl Valley Railway** now runs through the Sihl valley and has a station right at the Sihlwald.

Since about **2000**, the city of Zurich has given up harvesting timber in the Sihlwald. The forest is to develop naturally again. Trees may grow old, fall over and stay lying. In the long term, **more old trees** and **more dead wood** are therefore expected. Dead wood is very valuable, because fungi, beetles and many other living things live in it.

Together with the **Langenberg Wildlife Park** near Langnau am Albis, the Sihlwald forms the **Wildnispark Zürich**. In the Langenberg live animals that were once native to Switzerland or still are, such as deer, wild boar, wolves, bears and elk. In the Sihlwald you can discover wild nature along paths. A visitor centre explains the forest.

gewusst: As a “Nature Experience Park”, the Wildnispark Zürich Sihlwald is a Park of National Importance in Switzerland.
Because the Sihlwald is no longer tidied up, forest scenes are appearing again like those in primeval forests.

t1cxuns9.t: Test plantings of tree species for the future

teile.einleitung: Climate change is altering the conditions for Swiss forests. In the project “Test plantings of tree species for the future”, researchers are checking which trees can cope with the future climate. To do this, they plant different tree species at many places in Switzerland and observe them over a long time.
wichtigste: The main partners are the research institute WSL and the Federal Office for the Environment FOEN.
Cantonal forestry services and forest owners also take part.
The test sites are spread across the whole of Switzerland.
Native and foreign species are tested, for example Douglas fir, Atlas cedar and sweet chestnut.
Growth, survival and damage are recorded.
The trials last for decades, because trees live a very long time.

abschnitte.text: The project is run by the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research **WSL** and the Federal Office for the Environment **FOEN**. They work together with **cantonal forestry services** and forest owners. Together they test which tree species can cope with the future climate. The results should help foresters to plant the right trees. After all, a tree planted today still has to be healthy in many decades.

The test plantings are at many **sites** across Switzerland. They are spread over different altitudes, regions and soils. Some places already have a climate today that will only be found elsewhere in the future. That makes it possible to compare tree species under very **different conditions**. From this, it can be estimated which species can survive where.

Native and foreign tree species are tested. The **Douglas fir** comes from the west of North America and was brought to Europe in the 19th century. It grows quickly and is considered more tolerant of drought than the spruce. The **Atlas cedar** grows naturally in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco and Algeria. The **sweet chestnut** has shaped the south side of the Alps since Roman times and could become more important in the Central Plateau too if the climate gets warmer.

The researchers do not only measure how fast the trees grow. They also record exactly how many **survive**. Damage caused by **drought**, **late frost** and **pests** is important. A tree for the future has to endure heat and still survive cold nights in spring. Because trees often stand in the same place for over 100 years, trials like this last **decades**.

abschnitte.titel: Not all eggs in one basket
abschnitte.text: Behind the project is the principle of **spreading the risk**. If one tree species fails because of drought or pests, other species can keep the forest going. **Mixed forests** are therefore considered more resilient. This matters because the Swiss forest also protects against avalanches and rockfall. Nobody knows exactly what the climate will be like in 100 years.

gewusst: A test tree planted today may only give a finished result for the grandchildren of today’s researchers.
The sweet chestnut was probably encouraged by the Romans on the south side of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Dew is the little drops of water that glitter on grass, leaves and spider webs on cool mornings. It does not fall from the sky like rain, but forms right where it lies. That is why it is counted as deposited precipitation.
wichtigste: Dew is made of small drops of water that form on the grass on cool mornings.
Dew forms when damp air cools down on cold surfaces.
The water vapour in the air condenses into drops.
The temperature at which this happens is called the dew point.
There is most dew after clear, windless nights.
If it is below freezing, frost forms instead of dew.
Some plants and animals in deserts live on dew.

abschnitte.text: **Dew** is water that settles out of the invisible moisture in the air onto surfaces. You find it mostly early in the morning on meadows, car windows and spider webs. Because it does not fall from clouds, it is called **deposited precipitation**. Frost and hoarfrost also belong to this group.

On clear nights, the ground and plants give off heat into the sky and cool down a lot. The air directly above them cools down as well. Cold air can hold less water vapour than warm air. When it reaches the **dew point**, the water vapour turns into liquid water, which is called **condensation**.

abschnitte.titel: When is there a lot of dew?
abschnitte.text: Most dew forms after nights without clouds and without wind. Clouds act like a blanket and hold the heat in, so the ground stays warmer. Wind mixes the air and stops it from cooling down strongly near the ground. There is especially a lot of dew in late summer and autumn, when the air is damp and the nights are getting longer.

If the temperature of the surface is below freezing, no drops form, but fine ice crystals instead. This white coating is called **frost**. When drops of dew freeze afterwards, it is called frozen dew. In winter you often see frost on meadows, roofs and car windows.

Dew is an important source of water for many living things. In the Namib Desert in Africa, beetles catch drops of fog and dew on their backs and drink them. Snails and earthworms like to be out and about when the grass is wet with dew. The drops on the edges of leaves in the morning are often not dew at all, but water that the plant gives off itself, called **guttation**.

You experience the same principle when a cold bottle from the fridge gets wet on the outside. Glasses also mist up when you come into a warm room from outside in winter. The drops of dew on a field usually supply only very little water, less than a millimetre per night. Even so, meadows can be so wet in the morning that your shoes get soaked through.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which the water vapour in the air turns into drops
The change from water vapour to liquid water
Water as an invisible gas in the air
Ice crystals that form when it is freezing instead of dew

gewusst: Dew likes to form on blades of grass, because thin blades cool down especially quickly at night.
A desert beetle in the Namib stretches up into the fog in the morning so that drops of water run into its mouth.
People used to believe that dew fell from the sky like rain.

teile.einleitung: A keystone species is a species of animal or plant that is much more important to its ecosystem than its abundance would suggest. If it disappears, the whole community of living things changes greatly.
wichtigste: The term keystone species was coined by Robert Paine in 1969.
Without the sea star Pisaster, mussels spread and the number of species fell.
The influence of a keystone species is much greater than its abundance.
The beaver reshapes waters as an ecosystem engineer.
Elephants keep the savanna open.
Many other animals use the holes of the black woodpecker.

abschnitte.text: The American zoologist **Robert Paine** coined the term **keystone species** in 1969. He compared an especially influential species with the **keystone** of a stone arch. This stone at the top in the middle holds the whole arch together. A keystone species can be rare and yet shape the structure of a community of living things.

On the rocky coast in the north-west of the USA, Paine repeatedly removed the sea star **Pisaster** from the rocks. This sea star prefers to eat **mussels**. Without it, the mussels overgrew the rocks and crowded out many other species. The **number of species** fell clearly. In this way Paine showed how important a single predator can be.

The **beaver** was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. From the middle of the 20th century it was reintroduced. It is regarded as an **ecosystem engineer**: with dams it dams up streams and creates ponds, wetlands and **dead wood**. Many amphibians, insects and fish benefit from this. The **black woodpecker** is also important in Swiss forests. Its large holes are later used by, for example, stock doves, Tengmalm’s owls, bats or wild bees.

abschnitte.titel: Examples from all over the world
abschnitte.text: **African elephants** eat bushes and push over trees. In this way they prevent **scrub encroachment** and keep the savanna open. **Prairie dogs** in North America dig large burrow systems, loosen the soil and offer shelter to other animals. **Fig trees** in tropical forests bear fruit even in times of scarcity. They are therefore called a **keystone resource** for fruit-eating animals.

gewusst: A single beaver dam can turn a stream into a whole landscape of ponds.
Because fig trees fruit at different times, there are almost always ripe figs somewhere.

teile.einleitung: Moulds are tiny fungi that can grow on food, on walls and almost anywhere. Some are dangerous, others make famous cheeses. It is important to know how to deal with mould.
wichtigste: Moulds reproduce by spores in the air.
The invisible network of fungal threads can run through a whole loaf of bread.
Moulds can form poisonous mycotoxins.
Aflatoxin from spoiled nuts is regarded as strongly carcinogenic.
Noble mould gives Roquefort and Camembert their flavour.
Airing and correct heating help against mould on walls.

abschnitte.text: A mould consists of fine **fungal threads** that form a network. What we see as a green or grey patch is only the **spore bearers**. The network can spread invisibly through soft bread. That is why you should throw away a whole loaf with a patch of mould. With **hard cheese**, you can cut away a small spot generously, with about a centimetre of margin.

Moulds form huge numbers of tiny **spores**. These float in the air almost everywhere. If they land in a damp and nutritious place, they germinate and grow. That is why food goes mouldy especially fast when it is stored damp and warm. Cooling and dry storage slow the growth.

Many moulds form **mycotoxins**, that is, fungal poisons. They can do harm even in small amounts and are often not destroyed by cooking. **Aflatoxin** is especially dangerous. It is produced by fungi of the genus **Aspergillus** and can occur in spoiled nuts. You should therefore not eat nuts that smell musty or taste bitter.

Some moulds are very useful. The noble mould **Penicillium roqueforti** grows in the holes of **Roquefort** cheese and forms the blue-green veins. **Camembert** and Brie have a white, downy rind made of noble mould. **Grey mould** attacks strawberries and grapes in damp weather. On wine grapes, under certain conditions, it can even be wanted as **noble rot**.

Mould on walls forms where it is **damp** for a long time, for example in corners or behind furniture. When cooking, showering and breathing, a lot of water vapour gets into the air. By **airing in bursts**, that is, briefly with the windows wide open, damp air escapes outside. Correct **heating** keeps the walls warm and dry. That way mould has no chance.

gewusst: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered in a mould.
Mould spores are so small that individually you can only see them under the microscope.

teile.einleitung: Senescence means ageing. In plants it is not a random decay but an orderly programme. The best-known example is the autumn colouring of deciduous trees before the leaves fall.
wichtigste: Leaf senescence is an orderly, genetically controlled programme.
In it, the tree takes nutrients such as nitrogen back into the twigs and trunk.
Red autumn leaves arise from newly formed anthocyanins.
The leaf detaches at an abscission layer at the base of the leaf stalk.
The plant hormone ethylene greatly speeds up leaf ageing and leaf fall.
In central Europe, it is mainly the shortening days that trigger autumn senescence.
Monocarpic plants flower only once and die afterwards.

abschnitte.text: When a leaf is injured, it dies in a disorderly way. In **leaf senescence** it is different. It is an **orderly, genetically controlled programme**. The cells break down their components step by step. Only at the end does the leaf die. In deciduous trees in central Europe, autumn is triggered mainly by the **shortening days**, with cooler temperatures added to this.

A leaf contains valuable substances, above all **nitrogen** in the proteins. If the tree simply dropped its leaves, these would be lost. That is why, before leaf fall, it breaks down the green **chlorophyll** and many proteins. The nutrients are taken back into the **twigs and trunk** and used in spring for new leaves.

When the chlorophyll has been broken down, the yellow and orange **carotenoids**, which were in the leaf all along, become visible. Some trees, for example some **maple species**, also form new pigments in autumn, the **anthocyanins**. They colour the leaves bright red. Researchers suspect that they protect the leaf from too much light during the breakdown.

At the base of the leaf stalk, a special layer of cells forms, the **abscission layer**. There the cells separate from one another, and the leaf falls off. The wound is sealed with a layer of cork. The plant hormone **ethylene** speeds up leaf ageing and leaf fall especially strongly. Other hormones, the cytokinins, by contrast, delay ageing.

It is not only leaves that age. **Monocarpic** plants flower and fruit only once and then die completely. These include many annual plants such as wheat, but also some species of bamboo. In agriculture there are **stay-green varieties** whose leaves stay green longer thanks to delayed senescence. **Gregor Mendel** already studied a characteristic connected with this: the **yellow or green seed colour** of peas is based on a gene for the breakdown of chlorophyll.

gewusst: A single ripe apple gives off ethylene and can in this way make other fruits near it ripen faster.
Larches are conifers that turn their needles golden yellow in autumn and shed them, as deciduous trees do their leaves.

teile.einleitung: The floating-leaf zone is a belt in the shallow water of lakes and ponds. Plants grow here whose roots are in the bottom and whose leaves float on the surface of the water.
wichtigste: The floating-leaf zone lies lakewards of the reed belt in shallow water.
Typical are the white water lily and the yellow water lily.
Water lilies are anchored in the bed of the water.
Long, flexible stalks hold the leaves up, even when the water level changes.
The stomata lie on the upper surface of the leaf.
A layer of wax makes water bead off.

abschnitte.text: On the shore of a lake, plants grow in belts depending on the depth of the water. Close to land stands the **reed bed** with reeds. Further out follows the **floating-leaf zone**. Deeper still lies the **submerged zone**, where plants live entirely under water. Each zone has plants adapted to its depth of water.

The best-known plant of the floating-leaf zone is the **white water lily**. Also typical is the **yellow water lily** with its round, yellow flowers. Species such as floating pondweed are also found. These plants are anchored with rhizomes in the **bed of the water**. Not anchored is the tiny **duckweed**, which floats freely and can cover ponds like a green carpet.

abschnitte.titel: Leaves for life on the water
abschnitte.text: Floating leaves are specially built. Their **stomata** for gas exchange lie on the **upper surface of the leaf**, because the underside lies in the water. In land plants it is usually the other way round. A **layer of wax** on the upper side makes water bead off, so that the openings stay free. The leaves are leathery and do not tear easily.

In the muddy bottom there is little oxygen. That is why water lilies have an **air-filled tissue** in their stalks and leaves. It carries air from the leaves down to the roots. The **long, flexible leaf stalks** make sure that the leaves stay at the top, even when the water level rises or falls.

The floating leaves shade the water and offer shelter. **Frogs** like to sit on them, dragonflies land on them, and water snails crawl on the underside. Fish hide beneath them. In this way the floating-leaf zone is a rich habitat.

gewusst: The leaves of the tropical giant water lily Victoria can reach a diameter of about three metres.
Duckweeds are among the smallest flowering plants in the world.

teile.einleitung: Sieve tubes are the pipes in which plants transport sugar and other substances from the leaves to roots, fruits and buds. They form the most important part of the phloem, which is also called the sieve part.
wichtigste: Sieve tubes transport sugar from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Between the sieve tube elements lie cross walls with holes in them, the sieve plates.
The contents of working sieve tubes are under positive pressure.
When injured, P-proteins quickly plug the sieve tubes.
In trees, the working sieve tubes lie in the phloem of the inner bark.
The cambium constantly forms new sieve tubes.
Conifers have sieve cells instead of sieve tubes.

abschnitte.text: In the leaves the plant makes sugar by **photosynthesis**. But roots, buds and fruits need this too. The transport takes place in the **sieve tubes**. They belong to the **phloem**, the sieve part of the vascular bundles. Water and minerals, by contrast, rise from the roots in the **xylem**, the wood part. In a foliage leaf the phloem usually lies towards the **underside of the leaf**, and the xylem towards the upper side.

A sieve tube consists of many cells lying one behind another, the **sieve tube elements**. They are alive but no longer have a nucleus. Beside them lie small **companion cells** that supply them. Between two elements lie cross walls with holes in them, the **sieve plates**. Through their pores the sap flows from cell to cell, rather as through a sieve.

The contents of working sieve tubes are under **positive pressure**. Where sugar is pumped in, water flows in after it, and the pressure rises. Where sugar is used up, it falls. In this way the sap flows from a place of high pressure to a place of low pressure. If a sieve tube is injured, **P-proteins**, that is, phloem proteins, and the substance callose quickly plug it so that no sap leaks out.

abschnitte.titel: Sieve tubes in a tree trunk
abschnitte.text: In the trunk of a tree, between wood and bark, lies a thin forming tissue, the **cambium**. It produces wood on the inside and constantly produces new sieve tubes on the outside. The working sieve tubes lie in the **phloem**, the inner bark. If you remove a ring of bark all round the trunk, the phloem is interrupted. The **roots** then get no more sugar, and the tree usually dies.

**Conifers** and other gymnosperms have no true sieve tubes. They have **sieve cells** instead. These are longer and narrower and have no large sieve plates, but smaller sieve areas on the side walls. They fulfil the same task, however.

gewusst: Aphids pierce individual sieve tubes with their mouthparts. Researchers use severed aphid mouthparts to obtain pure sieve tube sap.
The sweet honeydew of aphids is basically sieve tube sap that has passed through the body of the aphid.

teile.einleitung: Below storage power stations, the water level in rivers often rises and falls several times a day. This change is called hydropeaking, with a surge and a low flow. It is a great burden for fish and small animals.
wichtigste: Hydropeaking arises when storage power stations are switched on and off.
The low flow is the low discharge when the turbines are stopped.
Young fish can be stranded on gravel banks when the water drops quickly.
In a surge, many bottom-dwelling animals are swept away.
Compensation basins dampen the fluctuations.
Since 2011, the Water Protection Act has required remediation.

abschnitte.text: **Storage power stations** collect water in reservoirs. They produce electricity mainly when a lot is needed. When the **turbines** run, a lot of water suddenly enters the river below the point of return. This high discharge is called the **surge**. When the turbines stand still, only the natural residual water flows. This low point is called the **low flow**.

If the water falls quickly, **young fish** are left behind in shallow areas. They get **stranded** on gravel banks that dry out and can dry up or be eaten. In a sudden surge, the strong current tears **invertebrates** from the bottom. This artificial **drift** thins out the populations. Fish eggs in the gravel can also be left dry.

abschnitte.titel: The surge to low flow ratio
abschnitte.text: To describe the strength of the fluctuations, the **surge discharge** is divided by the **low flow discharge**. If the surge is, for example, 60 cubic metres per second and the low flow 12 cubic metres per second, that gives 5 to 1. The greater this ratio, the more the river suffers. It is also important how fast the water level rises and falls.

Often a **compensation basin** is built. It takes in the turbine water and releases it more evenly to the river. In this way the fluctuations become smaller. Sometimes the water is also led directly into a lake or into a tunnel. In addition, riverbanks can be reshaped so that fish are not so easily stranded at low flow.

With the revision of the **Water Protection Act**, which came into force in 2011, power stations must **remediate** significant impairments caused by hydropeaking. The cantons plan where this is necessary. The costs are reimbursed to the operators from a **surcharge** on the transmission costs of the high-voltage grid. In the end, this is paid by all **electricity customers**.

gewusst: In some rivers the water level fluctuates several times a day because of power stations.
In Switzerland, hydropower supplies the largest part of domestically produced electricity.

teile.einleitung: The spongy mesophyll is a layer inside a foliage leaf. Its cells lie loosely, and between them there are many air spaces. In this way the plant can distribute gases in the leaf.
wichtigste: The spongy mesophyll consists of loose cells with air spaces.
The air spaces between the cells are called intercellular spaces.
They serve for gas exchange in the leaf.
Behind every stoma lies a sub-stomatal cavity.
Spongy mesophyll cells have fewer chloroplasts than palisade cells.
The layers from the top are: epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, epidermis.

abschnitte.text: A foliage leaf is built up of several layers. At the top lies the **epidermis** with a waxy protective layer, the **cuticle**. Below it follows the **palisade mesophyll** with long, densely packed cells. Then comes the **spongy mesophyll**. At the very bottom there is another epidermis, in which most of the **stomata** sit.

The cells of the spongy mesophyll are irregularly shaped and arranged **loosely**. Between them lie many air-filled cavities, the **intercellular spaces**. The term means “between the cells”. These spaces form a connected **air system** in the leaf. That is why the tissue recalls a sponge.

Through the stomata, **carbon dioxide** enters the leaf. Behind every stoma lies a **sub-stomatal cavity**. From there the air spreads into the intercellular spaces. **Oxygen** and **water vapour** leave by the same route. **Photosynthesis** also takes place in the spongy mesophyll, but its cells have fewer **chloroplasts** than the palisade cells.

If you put a foliage leaf in **hot water**, small air bubbles rise from the underside. The warmth makes the air in the cavities of the leaf **expand**. It escapes through the stomata. Because in most leaves these lie on the underside, you see the bubbles mainly on the **underside**.

In water plants the air spaces are often especially large. The leaves of the **water lily** float on the water because their leaf tissue has large, air-filled cavities. They give the leaf **buoyancy**. In water lilies the stomata lie on the upper surface of the leaf, because the underside is in the water.

gewusst: The air in a leaf is connected to the outside air through the intercellular spaces.
Many leaves are a paler green underneath because the spongy mesophyll has fewer chloroplasts.

teile.einleitung: The cowslip is a well-known spring flower with yellow blooms. It grows in meadows and at woodland edges. Its German name and an old legend tell of keys.
wichtigste: The cowslip has yellow flowers with small orange spots.
Several flowers hang at the top of the stem like a bunch of keys.
In German it is also called “Himmelsschlüssel”, the key of heaven.
It blooms mainly in April and May.
It belongs to the primulas.
According to a legend, Saint Peter dropped the keys of heaven.

abschnitte.text: The **cowslip** has **yellow** flowers. Inside they often have small **orange spots**. At the top of the stem **several flowers** sit together. They all lean to the same side. This recalls a bunch of keys. That is how the flower got its German name, “Schlüsselblume”, or key flower.

The cowslip belongs to the **primulas**. Related to it are the colourful primulas that people buy in pots in spring. The leaves lie as a rosette close to the ground. They are wrinkled and slightly hairy on the underside. It flowers in spring, mainly in **April** and **May**.

The cowslip likes to grow in sunny **meadows** and at **woodland edges**. In Switzerland you find it in the lowlands and in the mountains. Bumblebees and bees visit its flowers to drink nectar. Because many meadows are now heavily fertilised, it has become rarer in some places.

abschnitte.titel: The legend of the key of heaven
abschnitte.text: In German the cowslip is also called **Himmelsschlüssel**, the key of heaven. The name comes from an old **legend**. According to it, **Saint Peter** dropped the keys to heaven. Where they fell to the earth, cowslips grew. This is how people in the past explained the special shape of the flowers.

gewusst: The flowers of the cowslip have a slightly sweet scent.
The scientific name of the primulas comes from the Latin word for “the first”, because they bloom so early.

teile.einleitung: Deadly nightshade is one of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Its glossy black berries look like small cherries and are dangerous for children precisely because of that.
wichtigste: All parts of deadly nightshade are poisonous, especially the berries and roots.
The ripe berries are black, glossy and look like small cherries.
The bell-shaped flowers are brown-violet.
The plant grows about as tall as a person.
It often grows in woodland clearings and at woodland edges.
Poisoning makes the pupils very large.

abschnitte.text: Deadly nightshade is a strong perennial that grows up to about **1.5 metres** tall, so roughly as tall as a person. It has large, egg-shaped leaves. In summer it bears single, **bell-shaped flowers** in a brown-violet colour. From them develop **glossy black berries** that sit in a star-shaped green calyx. It belongs to the **nightshade family**, like the potato and the tomato.

Deadly nightshade likes to grow in bright places in the forest, for example in **woodland clearings**, on forest tracks and in places where trees have been felled. It likes nutrient-rich, often chalky soils. In Switzerland, too, it occurs in many woods. Anyone who goes walking in late summer may spot its berries.

The plant contains poisons such as **atropine**. Even a few berries can be life-threatening for a child. What is dangerous is that the berries taste sweetish and look tempting. Typical signs of poisoning are a red face, a dry mouth, restlessness and very **large pupils**. If you suspect poisoning, get help at once: in Switzerland, Tox Info Suisse gives advice round the clock on the number **145**.

The scientific name is **Atropa belladonna**. “Bella donna” means **beautiful woman** in Italian. In the past, women are said to have dripped the juice into their eyes because large pupils were considered beautiful. This was dangerous. Today eye doctors use highly diluted, precisely dosed active substances to widen the pupils for examinations.

gewusst: For some animals such as birds the berries are less dangerous, and they eat them and so spread the seeds.
The name “Atropa” goes back to Atropos, one of the goddesses of fate in Greek myth.

teile.einleitung: Besides sugar, proteins and fats, plants make many other substances. These secondary plant compounds are not needed directly for growing, but they help plants to protect themselves and to deal with their environment.
wichtigste: Secondary plant compounds are not directly necessary for growth and energy production.
Many serve to defend against herbivores and pathogens.
Alkaloids such as caffeine and nicotine contain nitrogen and are mostly basic.
Glucosinolates are typical of the cabbage family and release pungent mustard oils.
Capsaicin makes chilli peppers hot.
Phytoalexins are made by a plant only after an attack.

abschnitte.text: The **primary metabolism** includes substances that every plant needs to live, such as sugar from photosynthesis, proteins and fats. **Secondary plant compounds**, by contrast, are not directly necessary for growth and energy production. Even so, they are very important. They protect against enemies, attract pollinators or shield from strong sunlight. Tens of thousands of such substances are known.

Plants cannot run away. That is why they defend themselves with chemistry against **herbivores** and **pathogens**. Many substances taste bitter, are pungent or are poisonous. Some are made by plants all the time, others only when needed. **Phytoalexins**, for example, are made by a plant only after fungi or bacteria have attacked it.

**Alkaloids** are natural substances that contain nitrogen and are mostly basic. Many have a strong effect on animals and humans. Well-known examples are **caffeine** from coffee and tea and **nicotine** from the tobacco plant. The poison of deadly nightshade also belongs here. Some alkaloids are used as medicines, but many are poisonous.

Cabbage, mustard, radish and cress belong to the **cabbage family**. They contain **glucosinolates**. When chewed, these are broken down and release pungent **mustard oils**. That is why mustard burns in the nose. The heat of chilli peppers, by contrast, comes from the substance **capsaicin**. It deters many mammals, while birds hardly feel it.

**Saponins** can be recognised because when a plant solution is shaken with water, a **lasting foam** forms, similar to soap. **Cyanogenic glycosides** such as **amygdalin** in bitter almonds can release the poisonous gas **hydrogen cyanide**, also called prussic acid. Other secondary plant compounds are dyes such as the red and blue anthocyanins or fragrant substances such as the menthol of peppermint.

gewusst: Many medicines go back to secondary plant compounds, for example active substances from willow bark or foxglove.
The colour of blueberries, red cabbage and red autumn leaves comes from anthocyanins.

teile.einleitung: The fir and beech forest is a mixed forest of silver firs and beeches. In Switzerland it grows mainly in the Jura and the Pre-Alps, at middle altitudes. Sycamore maple is often found there too.
wichtigste: Silver fir and beech are the main trees in a fir and beech forest.
Sycamore maple is often mixed in.
In Switzerland it is widespread in the Jura and the Pre-Alps.
The silver fir can grow even in deep shade.
Roe deer and red deer browse young firs heavily.
The silver fir copes with drought better than the spruce.

abschnitte.text: In this forest, **silver fir** and **beech** grow together. **Sycamore maple** is often mixed in, as it likes damp soil rich in nutrients. In Switzerland you find forests like this especially in the **Jura** and the **Pre-Alps**. There the climate is damp and moderately cool. On the ground you often find **woodruff**, whose leaves grow in stars around the stem.

Young silver firs can **wait for decades in the shade** of old trees. They hardly grow at all in the meantime. As soon as light falls through a gap, they quickly shoot up. This ability makes the fir especially valuable for **mixed forests**. That way a forest develops with trees of every age.

The buds and shoots of young firs are very popular with **roe deer** and red deer. This nibbling is called **browsing**. Where too much game lives, young firs are often missing. The forest then slowly loses its silver firs. That is why foresters and hunters try to keep forest and game in balance.

During the **forest dieback** of the 1980s, the silver fir was thought to be especially sensitive to air pollution. People spoke of “fir dieback”. Today, with **climate change**, foresters are relying on it more again. Thanks to its deep roots, it can still reach water in dry summers. It copes with drought better than the **spruce**.

The wood of the silver fir is practically **resin-free**. Unlike spruce, pine or larch, it has no resin canals. That is why it is well suited to barrels, **wood panelling** and building parts that should not ooze resin. Silver firs are among the tallest trees in Europe. Their bark is light grey, which is where the name comes from.

gewusst: The cones of the silver fir stand upright on the branches and fall apart while still on the tree.
Dried woodruff smells of hay.

teile.einleitung: The elder is a common shrub at woodland edges, in hedges and in gardens. In Switzerland it is often called “Holder”. Its flowers and berries have long been used in the kitchen.
wichtigste: The elder blooms in May and June with white flowers.
The flower clusters look like large, flat plates.
Ripe elderberries are black-violet.
You must not eat the berries raw, only cooked.
Inside the twigs there is white, soft pith.
Birds like to eat the berries.

abschnitte.text: The elder grows as a large shrub or small tree and reaches several metres in height. You find it at **woodland edges**, in **hedges**, by paths and often near farms. In Switzerland it is often called **Holder** or Holderbusch. It grows fast and is very undemanding.

The elder blooms in **May and June**. Many small white to cream flowers sit together in large, **flat flower clusters** that look like plates. They have a strong, sweetish scent. From the flowers people make **elderflower cordial**, or they dip them in batter and fry them as “Holderküchlein”, elderflower fritters.

In late summer small, **black-violet berries** ripen. Raw they are not tolerated, because they contain a substance that can cause nausea and stomach ache. You should not eat unripe berries, leaves or stalks either. By **cooking**, the substance is made harmless. From cooked berries you can make **jam**, juice or jelly. The juice, by the way, stains strongly.

For many **birds** such as blackbirds, starlings and blackcaps, the berries are a popular food. The birds excrete the seeds again in other places. In this way the elder soon grows in new spots. The flowers are visited by insects, and in the dense shrub small animals find shelter.

If you cut an elder twig through, you see **white, soft pith** inside. It can be pushed out easily. In the past, children made whistles and little tubes from it. In folk belief the elder was regarded as a protective tree that was supposed to bring luck to house and farm.

gewusst: The light elder pith used to be used in science to make very thin slices of plants for the microscope.
The scientific name of the elder is Sambucus nigra, and “nigra” means black in Latin.

teile.einleitung: Guard cells are special cells in the skin of a leaf. Always two of them surround a small gap, the stoma. They decide when the plant takes in gases and gives off water.
wichtigste: A typical stoma consists of two guard cells.
When opening, they mainly take up potassium ions, and water flows in after them.
Abscisic acid makes the stomata close in drought.
Blue light is an effective signal to open.
Guard cells have chloroplasts, but the other epidermal cells mostly do not.
In grasses the guard cells are dumbbell-shaped.

abschnitte.text: The **epidermis** is the outer layer of cells of a leaf. In it lie many tiny **stomata**. Each one is surrounded by **two** curved **guard cells**. Through the gap, carbon dioxide gets into the leaf, and oxygen and water vapour get out. Unlike most of the colourless epidermal cells, guard cells contain **chloroplasts**.

To open, the guard cells use **proton pumps** to pump hydrogen ions outwards. Then **potassium ions** flow in. Water follows by **osmosis**, and the internal pressure, the **turgor**, rises. The cell wall facing the gap is thicker and less stretchy. In addition, the cellulose fibres run radially away from the gap. That is why the cells curve as they swell and move apart.

**Blue light** in particular acts as a signal to open. Blue light receptors activate the proton pumps, and in the morning the gaps open. When **water is short**, the plant makes the hormone **abscisic acid**. It causes the guard cells to lose ions and water, and the gap closes. A lot of **carbon dioxide** in the leaf also leads to closing, and in this way the plant saves water.

In many plants the guard cells are bean-shaped or kidney-shaped. Grasses such as **wheat** and **maize** have **dumbbell-shaped** guard cells with a thick middle and thin ends. They open and close especially fast. In many plants there are also **subsidiary cells** next to the guard cells. They exchange ions with the guard cells and support their movement.

gewusst: In most foliage leaves the stomata lie mainly on the underside.
Thousands of stomata can sit on a single leaf.

teile.einleitung: The tea plant provides the leaves for black, green and white tea. Its botanical name is Camellia sinensis and it is related to the camellia. The tea culture originally comes from China.
wichtigste: The botanical name of the tea plant is Camellia sinensis.
For tea, mainly young leaves and buds are picked.
Black tea is oxidised, green tea is not.
China produces the most tea in the world, followed by India.
Darjeeling and Assam are well-known tea regions in India.
Peppermint tea is not real tea, because it does not come from the tea plant.

abschnitte.text: The botanical name of the tea plant is **Camellia sinensis**. It is related to the **camellias** that you know as ornamental plants. In the wild it can grow into a tree of over ten metres. On **plantations** it is cut back regularly so that it stays about hip height. That way the pickers can easily reach the shoots.

For tea, mainly the **shoot tips** are picked: the bud and the two youngest leaves. They make the finest tea. A tea plant can be picked again and again for many years. Tea grows well in warm, damp areas, often on mountain slopes. In Switzerland there is even a small tea garden on **Monte Verità** near Ascona.

Black and green tea come from the same plant. For **black tea**, the rolled leaves are left to react with oxygen. This is called **oxidation**, and the leaves turn dark. For **green tea**, the leaves are heated quickly so that this does not happen. **Matcha** is a Japanese green tea made from shaded leaves, ground into a fine powder and whisked with water.

**China** is the country where tea culture began and today harvests by far the most tea. In second place comes **India**. There the **Darjeeling** is well known, named after a town at the foot of the Himalayas. **Assam** is an Indian state in the lowlands. Tea from Sri Lanka is still called **Ceylon tea**, because the island was called Ceylon until 1972.

Only an infusion from the tea plant counts as **real tea**. Infusions made from peppermint, camomile or fruit are called **herbal tea** or fruit tea. Real tea contains **caffeine**, which keeps you awake. Herbal teas mostly contain no caffeine. In Switzerland people enjoy both, especially in winter.

gewusst: Growing wild, a tea plant can reach over ten metres in height.
Black, green and white tea all come from the same plant, only the processing is different.

teile.einleitung: Animals leave signs everywhere, even if we rarely see them. Signs like these are called **animal tracks**. If you can read them, you can find out who was out and about in the forest or on the meadow.
wichtigste: Animal tracks are especially easy to see in fresh snow.
In summer, footprints are easy to find in soft mud.
The hare leaves two long and two small prints.
The roe deer leaves two narrow halves of a hoof.
In a cat’s track you see no claws, in a dog’s track you do.
Gnawed cones, droppings and slime trails are also animal tracks.

abschnitte.text: You see tracks best in **fresh snow**, on the morning after a snowy night. In summer it is worth looking at **soft mud** at the edge of a stream or in puddles on a forest path. Each print is called a **footprint**. Several footprints one behind the other make a **trail**. From it you can tell whether an animal walked, jumped or ran.

The **hare** hops so that its long hind paws land in front of its short front paws. This produces **two long and two small prints**. The **roe deer** is an even-toed ungulate: you see **two narrow halves of a hoof** that meet in a point at the front. The **fox**, when walking, puts its hind paw exactly into the print of its front paw. The tracks therefore lie **almost in a line**, as if strung on a thread. Hunters call this “schnüren” (lacing).

Cats and dogs both have four toes and a pad. The **cat** draws in its claws when walking, so you see **no claws** in the print. With the **dog** and the fox, the claws can usually be seen. Many **birds** leave tracks with **three toes pointing forwards** and often one pointing back. Hopping birds such as sparrows make prints in pairs side by side.

Animal tracks also include **feeding signs**. A spruce cone that has been gnawed down to the spindle and looks ragged often comes from a squirrel. Mice gnaw cones much more neatly. Droppings, feathers, hairs on fences or holes in the ground also give animals away. The **snail** leaves a **shiny slime trail** on the path, which glistens in the sun.

gewusst: When fleeing, a hare can make jumps of several metres, and you can see this from the wide gaps between the tracks.
You can take animal tracks from the mud home as a souvenir by making plaster casts.

teile.einleitung: Taxines are poisonous substances from the yew. They are found in almost all parts of the tree and act mainly on the heart. The yew is an evergreen conifer that can live to a very great age.
wichtigste: Taxines are the poison of the yew, scientific name Taxus.
Taxine mainly disturbs the rhythm of the heart.
Yews can be over 1000 years old.
There are male and female yews.
Only female yews bear seeds with a red fleshy covering.
The cancer drug paclitaxel was discovered in the Pacific yew.

abschnitte.text: The yew is called **Taxus** in science, which is why its poison is called **taxine**. It is an **evergreen** conifer with soft, dark green needles. The yew grows very slowly and can live to be over **1000 years** old. It puts up with a lot of shade. That is why it often stands in gardens, parks and cemeteries, in Switzerland too.

Taxines are found in the needles, bark, wood and seeds of the yew. They act mainly on the **heart** and disturb its rhythm. In severe poisoning the heart can stop. Even a few needles can be dangerous for people. **Horses** are especially sensitive, and the yew is very poisonous to them.

The yew is **dioecious**: male and female flowers grow on different trees. Only female yews produce seeds with a red, sweet **aril**. This covering is the only part without poison. The seed inside it, however, is poisonous. Birds eat the covering and pass the hard seed out undigested, and in this way they spread the yew.

For **roe deer**, the yew is far less dangerous than for horses. They even like to nibble the young shoots. This harms young yews in the forest, because they grow so slowly. That is why in many forests there are hardly any young yews. Foresters sometimes protect them with fences.

In the bark of the **Pacific yew** from North America, a substance was found that is now used as a cancer drug: **paclitaxel**. Like other cell poisons, it slows the growth of cancer cells. Today the substance is mostly made from the needles of cultivated yews or by other methods. That way the trees no longer have to be felled.

gewusst: The bow of the glacier mummy Ötzi was made of yew wood.
Yew wood is very tough and springy, which is why many bows were made from it in the past.

teile.einleitung: Reed is a very large grass that grows by lakes, by rivers and in marshes. It often forms dense stands on the bank. For many animals this is an important habitat.
wichtigste: Reed belongs to the true grasses, like wheat.
It can grow about four metres tall.
The stem is hollow inside like a little tube.
A wide strip of reed on the bank is called a reed belt.
The reed warbler builds its nest between reed stems.
Thatched roofs are made from reed.

abschnitte.text: The **common reed** is a very large **grass**. It belongs to the **true grasses**, like wheat. Reed can grow about four metres tall, more than twice as tall as an adult. The stem is **hollow** inside, like a little tube. That is why the plant is also called reed cane.

In late summer, a soft, feathery **flower cluster**, a **panicle**, sits at the top of the stem. It sways in the wind. In autumn the reed becomes dry and **light brown**. The dry stems often stay standing all winter. In spring new green shoots grow from the ground.

abschnitte.titel: The reed belt as a habitat
abschnitte.text: On the bank, reed often grows so densely that it lies like a **reed belt** around the lake. Many animals find shelter there: fish, dragonflies, frogs and birds. The **reed warbler** weaves its nest between several reed stems. In Switzerland there are large reed areas, for example on **Lake Neuchâtel** and on **Lake Constance**. Bank vegetation such as reed is protected by law in Switzerland.

Underground, reed has long shoots and a dense **root network**. With these it spreads and holds the soil firm. Reed also slows down the **waves**. In this way it protects the bank from being washed away. Reed can even filter pollutants out of the water, which is why it is used in some constructed reed bed treatment plants.

People have used reed for a long time. **Thatched roofs** are made from reed. Such roofs keep out the rain and insulate well. Mats, fences and screens are also made from reed. In the past, simple flutes were even carved from the hollow stems.

gewusst: Reed is among the most widely distributed plants on Earth.
Underground, a stand of reed can form a huge connected network.

teile.einleitung: Chives are a popular kitchen herb with thin, hollow stems. They taste mildly of onion and grow back every year. In Switzerland they even grow wild in the Alps.
wichtigste: Chives have thin, round stems that are hollow inside.
You cut the stems off a few centimetres above the ground.
The flowers are pink to violet and edible.
Chives are perennial and sprout anew in spring.
You add them to the food only at the end so that they keep their flavour.
Wild chives grow in the Alps.

abschnitte.text: **Chives** have thin, **tube-shaped** stems. Inside they are **hollow**. They are related to onion, leek and garlic. That is why they taste like a mild **leek**. Their German name, “Schnittlauch”, means “cutting leek”, because you cut them into small **rolls** and sprinkle them over food.

You cut the stems off with **scissors** a few centimetres above the ground. After that **new stems** grow back. In this way you can harvest again and again all summer. Chives grow in the garden, in a pot on the balcony or on the windowsill.

In early summer chives form small **balls** of flowers. They are **pink to violet**. The flowers are **edible** and taste mildly of onion. You can use them to decorate a salad. Bees and bumblebees like to visit the flowers.

Chives taste best **fresh**. If you cook them, their **aroma** is lost. That is why they are mostly added to the food only at the end. They go well with scrambled eggs, potatoes, soups and quark. A slice of bread with butter and chives is a simple mid-morning snack, or “Znüni” in Swiss German.

Chives are **perennial**. In winter they withdraw into the ground and sprout anew in **spring**. In Switzerland they also grow **wild in the Alps**, for example in damp spots in mountain meadows. Wild chives often have a somewhat stronger flavour.

gewusst: You can freeze chives, and then they stay fresh for longer.
A chive plant can grow in the same place for many years.

teile.einleitung: Water lilies are water plants with large, round leaves that float on ponds and lakes. Their beautiful flowers open in the daytime and close again in the evening.
wichtigste: Water lilies grow in the water of ponds and lakes.
The white water lily has white flowers.
A long, flexible stalk joins the leaf to the rhizome on the bottom.
The leaf is round with a notch.
The flowers are open in the daytime.
Drops of water bead off the leaf.

abschnitte.text: Water lilies grow in the still water of **ponds and lakes**. Their **rhizome** sits in the muddy bottom. From there a **long, flexible stalk** grows up to the surface of the water. At the top the large leaf floats. If the water rises, the stalk gives way, and the leaf stays at the top all the same.

A water lily leaf is **round** and has a **notch**, so that it looks a bit like a cake with a piece missing. The upper surface is smooth and glossy. When raindrops fall on it, they **bead off** and roll down as little balls. This comes from a fine layer of wax.

The **white water lily** has large, **white flowers** with a yellow heart. In the morning they open, and in the evening they close again. So the flowers are open **in the daytime**. There are also water lilies with pink, red or yellow flowers, especially in garden ponds.

A **frog** likes to sit on the large leaves and sun itself or wait for insects. Dragonflies also rest on them. Under the leaves, fish find shade and shelter. The **yellow water lily** looks similar to the water lily but has smaller, **yellow** flowers.

gewusst: The painter Claude Monet painted a great many pictures of water lilies in his garden in France.
The leaves of the tropical giant water lily grow so big that a small child could lie on them.

teile.einleitung: In pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of a flower. If the pollen comes from the same plant, this is called self-pollination. Many crop plants such as the pea pollinate themselves in this way.
wichtigste: In self-pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of the same plant.
The pea mostly pollinates itself.
Advantage: self-pollination works even without pollinators.
Disadvantage: over many generations, genetic diversity decreases.
Cleistogamous flowers do not open and pollinate themselves in the bud.
With self-pollinating peas, Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of heredity.

abschnitte.text: A flower has **stamens**, which make pollen, and a **pistil** with a sticky **stigma** at the top. In **cross-pollination**, insects or the wind bring pollen from another plant. In **self-pollination**, pollen reaches the stigma of the **same plant**, often even of the same flower. After that a seed can develop.

Many crop plants mostly pollinate themselves, for example the **pea**, the bean, wheat and barley. In the pea this often happens before the flower has properly opened. **Tomato flowers** also pollinate themselves when the pollen is shaken out. In greenhouses, **bumblebees** are used for this. With their buzzing they make the flowers vibrate.

Some plants form **cleistogamous flowers**. These do not open at all and pollinate themselves in the closed bud. One example is the **violet**. In spring it bears beautiful, open flowers for insects. Later in the year it also forms inconspicuous, closed flowers that reliably produce seeds.

A great **advantage**: self-pollination works even **without pollinators**, for example in bad weather or in areas with few insects. A **disadvantage** shows over many generations: **genetic diversity decreases**. The plants become very similar to one another and can adapt less well to changes. Some plants are therefore **self-sterile**: their own pollen on the stigma does not lead to fertilisation.

In the 19th century the monk **Gregor Mendel** studied thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden in Brno. Because peas pollinate themselves, he was able to breed pure varieties and cross them deliberately. In doing so he observed how characteristics such as flower colour or seed shape are passed on. In this way he discovered the **laws of heredity**.

gewusst: Mendel’s discoveries received hardly any attention in his lifetime and were only rediscovered around 1900.
Bumblebees can “shake” pollen out of flowers by making their flight muscles vibrate rapidly.

teile.einleitung: Horsetails are ancient plants without flowers. Their stem can be pulled apart and pushed together again. Their relatives grew as tall as trees many millions of years ago.
wichtigste: The stem consists of sections that fit into each other like boxes.
The stem is hollow inside.
Horsetails contain hard silica and feel rough.
In the past they were used to scour pewter dishes, so they are also called pewterwort.
They reproduce with spores, not with seeds.
Hard coal was partly formed from the ancient forests with giant horsetails.

abschnitte.text: The stem of the horsetail is divided into separate **sections**. They fit into each other like small boxes. You can pull them apart and push them back in. That is how the plant got its German name, “Schachtelhalm”, from “Schachtel”, meaning box. Inside, the stem is **hollow**.

In many horsetails, thin **side branches** grow in a ring around the stem. This makes the plant look a little like a small fir tree. In the **field horsetail**, brownish shoots grow first in early spring. At their tip sits a **cone** with spores. Only after that come the green shoots with the side branches.

There is a lot of **silica** in the horsetail. This is a hard substance, like that found in sand. That is why the plant feels rough. In the past it was used to scour **pewter dishes** until they shone, like a scouring agent. That is why the horsetail is also called **pewterwort**.

Horsetails have no flowers and no seeds. They reproduce with **spores**, very fine grains that the wind spreads. Like the **ferns**, they belong to the **spore plants**. Many species grow in damp places, by ditches, in marshes or in fields. With their underground shoots they also spread through the soil.

Many millions of years ago there were relatives of the horsetails as tall as trees, the **calamites**. They usually grew up to 10 metres tall, and some even taller. They grew in large **swamp forests**. The plants of these forests were pressed together underground. Over a very long time, **hard coal** formed from them.

gewusst: Horsetails existed long before the dinosaurs.
Today’s horsetails are the last representatives of a once large group of plants.

teile.einleitung: Not everything we call a fruit is botanically a true fruit. In an accessory fruit, other parts of the flower grow along too, for example the receptacle. Apple, strawberry and rose hip are well-known examples.
wichtigste: A true fruit develops only from the ovary.
In an accessory fruit, other parts of the flower are also involved.
In the apple, only the core is the actual fruit.
Apple, pear and quince form a pome.
The red flesh of the strawberry develops from the receptacle.
The rose hip is the red accessory fruit of the rose.

abschnitte.text: In the middle of a flower sits the **ovary**. In a **true fruit**, only this part develops further, for example in the cherry. In an **accessory fruit**, other parts grow into the fruit as well. Often this is the **receptacle**, sometimes also the flower stalk or a whole flower cluster.

The juicy flesh of the apple grows from the **receptacle**. Only the parchment-like **core** with the pips comes from the ovary. Apple, pear and quince form this special accessory fruit, which is called a **pome**. In Switzerland, apples and pears are the most important **pome fruit**.

In the **strawberry**, the receptacle swells strongly after flowering and turns red and sweet. The small yellow dots on the surface are the actual fruitlets, tiny **nutlets**. In the wild rose, the jug-shaped receptacle forms a red shell. This accessory fruit is called a **rose hip**. Inside are many hard nutlets with fine hairs that itch on the skin.

On the **cashew tree**, the stalk below the fruit thickens into a juicy **cashew apple**. The actual fruit is the kidney-shaped nut that hangs from it. The **fig** is a jug-shaped **flower cluster** with the flowers sitting inside. From them develop many tiny fruitlets that crunch when you eat them.

gewusst: Children used to use the hairs from rose hips as itching powder.
Botanically, a strawberry is not a berry but an aggregate fruit made of many nutlets.

teile.einleitung: A snowflake is a small structure made of ice crystals that falls from the sky. Most snowflakes have six corners or six arms. Because every flake meets different conditions on its way, none looks exactly like another.
wichtigste: Snowflakes mostly have six corners or arms.
The hexagonal shape comes from the arrangement of the water molecules in ice.
A flake often consists of many crystals stuck together.
Its shape depends on temperature and humidity.
Snowflakes fall slowly, at about one metre per second.
Two completely identical large snowflakes are practically never found.

abschnitte.text: A snowflake is either a single **ice crystal** or several crystals that stick together. It forms in clouds when water vapour freezes on a tiny speck of dust. This little grain is called a **condensation nucleus**. As it falls, the crystal goes on growing and forms its typical shape.

When water molecules freeze, they join in a very particular pattern. This **crystal lattice** is hexagonal, like the cells of a honeycomb. That is why ice crystals grow with six corners or six arms. This even shape is called **symmetry**.

Depending on temperature and humidity, very different shapes grow. At about minus 15 degrees, especially beautiful **stars** with branching arms form. At other temperatures, flat plates, columns or fine needles form. Because each flake takes its own path through the cloud, each one is a little different.

The American **Wilson Bentley** was one of the first to photograph snowflakes through a microscope, from 1885. He took over 5,000 pictures and found no two alike. In the 1930s the Japanese researcher Ukichiro Nakaya grew snow crystals in the laboratory. He showed how temperature and humidity determine the shape.

Most snowflakes are only a few millimetres across. At temperatures around zero degrees, many crystals stick together into large, soft **flakes**. Snowflakes sink slowly, usually at about one metre per second. That is why they seem to dance through the air when it snows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regularly built piece of frozen water.
When a shape looks the same on all sides.
A speck of dust on which water freezes or gathers.
The ordered arrangement of the particles in a crystal.
