gewusst: Wilson Bentley was given the nickname “Snowflake Bentley”.
The largest flakes form at temperatures just around zero degrees, when many damp crystals stick together.
Snowflakes are actually transparent, and only look white because of scattered light.

teile.einleitung: Every living thing needs certain conditions, for example the right temperature or enough water. The **range of tolerance** shows the range of an environmental factor in which a species can survive. This knowledge helps us to understand where plants and animals are found.
wichtigste: The range of tolerance shows where a species can survive with regard to an environmental factor.
At the optimum, a living thing thrives best.
Near the limits lies the pessimum: survival yes, growth hardly.
A typical tolerance curve is bell-shaped.
Species with a narrow range of tolerance are called stenoecious, adaptable ones euryoecious.
According to Liebig, the scarcest factor limits growth.

abschnitte.text: You can measure how well a species lives at different values of a factor, for example temperature. If you put this in a diagram, a **bell-shaped curve** usually results. In the middle lies the **optimum**, where the species grows best. On both sides follows the **pessimum**: the species just about survives there, but hardly grows. Outside the range of tolerance it dies.

Species with a **narrow** range of tolerance are called **stenoecious**. The **brown trout**, for example, needs cool water rich in oxygen. If a stream gets too warm, it becomes dangerous for it. Species with a **wide** range of tolerance are called **euryoecious**. The **red fox** is a good example: it lives in the forest, on fields, in the mountains and even in the middle of Swiss cities.

Because stenoecious species only occur under certain conditions, they reveal something about their site. They are called **indicator species**. A dense stand of **stinging nettles** points to **soil rich in nitrogen**, for example next to a manure heap. Other plants indicate acid soil or lime. Experts use indicator species like these to assess soils and waters.

The German chemist **Justus von Liebig** described the **law of the minimum** in the 19th century. It says: the factor that is scarcest limits growth. People often imagine it with a barrel made of wooden staves. The water spills over at the shortest stave, no matter how long the others are. If a plant lacks potassium, for example, a lot of nitrogen fertiliser does not help either.

gewusst: Because the brown trout only lives in cool, clean water, it is regarded as an indicator species for good water quality.
The picture with the barrel is also called the “minimum barrel”.

teile.einleitung: The **titan arum** has one of the largest flower clusters in the whole plant kingdom. It grows in the rainforest of the island of Sumatra. When it flowers, it smells of rotting meat.
wichtigste: The titan arum comes from the island of Sumatra in Indonesia.
Its flower cluster can be over 3 metres tall.
It flowers only every few years and then only for about 1 to 2 days.
When flowering it smells of carrion and even becomes warm.
Under the ground it has a huge tuber.
In years without flowers it grows only a single, huge leaf.

abschnitte.text: The titan arum grows wild only in the tropical rainforest of the island of **Sumatra** in Indonesia. It belongs to the **arum family**. This also includes the cuckoo pint, which grows in Swiss forests but is much smaller. In nature the titan arum has become rare, because its rainforest is shrinking. Many botanical gardens around the world now grow it in large greenhouses.

What looks like a single giant flower is a **flower cluster** made of many small flowers. In the middle stands a long spadix, and around it a large, collar-like bract. The flower cluster can grow **over 3 metres** tall. Under the ground sits a **huge tuber**, which can weigh more than 100 kilograms. In it the plant stores nutrients for many years.

The titan arum flowers only **every few years**, and a flower cluster is open for only about **1 to 2 days**. Then it smells strongly **of rotting meat**. The smell attracts **insects**, mainly carrion beetles and flies, which otherwise look for dead meat. They carry pollen from plant to plant. The spadix **becomes warm** and in this way helps to spread the scent far into the air.

In the years without flowers, the tuber sends up **a single, huge leaf**. It looks like a small tree with a thick stalk and an umbrella of many leaf parts. The leaf can grow several metres tall. It carries out photosynthesis and fills the tuber with reserves again. Only when enough energy is stored can the plant flower again.

gewusst: When a titan arum flowers in a botanical garden, it is an event that people queue up for.
In Indonesian the titan arum is called “Bunga bangkai”, which means corpse flower.

teile.einleitung: A black hole is an object in space with such strong gravity that not even light can escape. That is why it is itself invisible and black. Even so, researchers can detect black holes, because they strongly influence their surroundings.
wichtigste: Nothing can escape from a black hole, not even light.
The boundary beyond which there is no going back is called the event horizon.
Many black holes form when very massive stars collapse in on themselves.
At the centre of almost every large galaxy sits a supermassive black hole.
At the centre of the Milky Way lies the black hole Sagittarius A*.
In 2019 the first picture of the shadow of a black hole was published.

abschnitte.text: A black hole is a place in space where a great deal of mass is squeezed together into a very small space. As a result the **gravity**, that is, the force of attraction, is extremely strong. Beyond a certain boundary, the **event horizon**, nothing can escape any more. What falls in is gone for ever.

Very massive stars burn up their fuel at the end of their lives. Then their core collapses under its own weight, often accompanied by a **supernova**. If enough mass remains, a **stellar black hole** forms, which is several to dozens of times as heavy as the Sun. How the giant black holes in the centres of galaxies became so large is still being researched.

abschnitte.titel: Giants at the centre of galaxies
abschnitte.text: At the heart of the Milky Way sits **Sagittarius A***, which has about four million times as much mass as the Sun. Such giants are called supermassive black holes. For showing that such a compact object is located there, Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020. Roger Penrose received the prize in the same year for the theory behind it.

You cannot see a black hole itself, but you can see its effect. Gas swirling around it forms a hot **accretion disc** that glows brightly. Stars nearby orbit strikingly fast around an invisible point. Since 2015, detectors have also measured **gravitational waves**, which arise when two black holes merge.

The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes all over the world into one giant telescope. In April 2019 it showed the first picture of a black hole, in the galaxy M87. You see a glowing ring with a dark **shadow** in the middle. In 2022 a picture followed of Sagittarius A* in our Milky Way.

Albert Einstein already described, with his **theory of relativity** of 1915, how mass curves space. From this it followed that black holes can exist. Stephen Hawking showed that they could give off radiation very slowly. The nearest known black hole lies over 1,500 light years away, so there is no danger for the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction with which masses attract each other.
The invisible boundary beyond which nothing can come back.
A hot, glowing disc of gas that swirls around a black hole.
The distance that light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

gewusst: If the Earth were squeezed into a black hole, it would be only about as big as a marble.
Near a black hole, time passes more slowly than far away from it.
The name “black hole” became known in the 1960s through the physicist John Wheeler.

teile.einleitung: The Shannon index is a number with which ecologists measure the diversity of a community of living things. It takes into account not only how many species occur, but also how evenly they are distributed.
wichtigste: The formula is H = -Σ pᵢ · ln pᵢ.
pᵢ is the share of species i among all individuals.
The index originally comes from information theory.
If only one species occurs, H is equal to 0.
For a given number of species S, H is greatest when all species are equally common.
The maximum value is ln S, so for four species about 1.39.
Pielou’s evenness is calculated as J = H / ln S.

abschnitte.text: The index goes back to the American mathematician **Claude Shannon**. In the 1940s he developed **information theory**, which describes how much information a message contains. Ecology later took over his formula to measure **biodiversity**. People also speak of the Shannon-Wiener index.

The Shannon index is calculated like this: **H = -Σ pᵢ · ln pᵢ**. Here **pᵢ** is the share of a species among all the individuals counted, and **ln** is the natural logarithm. The sign Σ means: you work out the expression for each species and add everything up. Because shares are smaller than 1, their logarithm is negative. The minus sign in front of the sum therefore makes H positive. Sometimes other logarithms are used, and then the numerical values change.

If **only a single species** occurs on an area, its share is 1. Since ln 1 is equal to 0, **H = 0**: no diversity. With **two equally common species**, each has a share of 0.5. Then H = ln 2, which is about **0.69**. If three species have the shares **0.5, 0.25 and 0.25**, the result is H = 0.5 · ln 2 + 2 · 0.25 · ln 4, which is roughly **1.04**.

For the same number of species **S**, the Shannon index reaches its **maximum value** when **all species are equally common**. This maximum value is **ln S**. For four species it is ln 4, which is about **1.39**. To see how close a community comes to this ideal, you calculate **Pielou’s evenness**: **J = H / ln S**. J lies between 0 and 1. A value close to 1 means that the species are distributed very evenly.

gewusst: A meadow with ten species, one of which covers almost everything, can have a smaller Shannon index than a meadow with five equally common species.
If you calculate with the logarithm to base 2, the Shannon index measures information in the unit of bits.

teile.einleitung: Terra preta is an especially dark and fertile soil in the Amazon region. The name is Portuguese and means “black earth”. It did not form naturally, but through people who lived there long ago.
wichtigste: Terra preta means “black earth”.
It is found in patches in the Amazon region, often by rivers.
It was formed by human settlements with charcoal and waste.
Typical finds in it are pieces of pottery.
The natural soils of the Amazon are mostly poor in nutrients.
The soils come from pre-Columbian cultures.

abschnitte.text: The rainforest on the **Amazon** looks very lush. Even so, its natural soils are mostly **heavily weathered and poor in nutrients**. High temperatures and heavy rainfall wash the nutrients out. Most of the nutrients are in the plants themselves and not in the soil. All the more astonishing are the patches of very fertile **terra preta**.

The Portuguese name **terra preta** means “black earth”. It describes the strikingly dark colour of these soils. They differ clearly from the light, reddish or yellowish soils around them. They are often found along **rivers**, where larger settlements used to be. Around the terra preta there is often the lighter, brownish **terra mulata**.

Terra preta is an **anthropogenic soil**, which means that people created it. **Charcoal**, kitchen waste and other remains built up around the settlements over a long time. **Bones** and fish remains brought a lot of phosphorus into the soil. Typical are numerous pieces of **pottery**, which show that people lived there. The terra mulata probably formed on former fields around the villages.

Most terra preta soils come from **pre-Columbian cultures**, that is, from the time before the Europeans arrived. They show that larger settled communities once lived in the Amazon region. For a long time it was thought that the rainforest had hardly been settled. Today experts are investigating how similarly fertile soils could be made using **biochar**.

gewusst: The charcoal in terra preta can hold on to nutrients and water like a sponge.
Terra preta is still fertile today, even though it formed centuries ago.

teile.einleitung: A compost heap gets surprisingly hot inside. This hot period is called the **thermophilic phase** or hot composting. It is important so that garden waste turns into clean, good compost.
wichtigste: The thermophilic phase is the hot phase of composting.
In the core of a well-built heap it gets about 50 to 70 °C.
It is preceded by the mesophilic phase with moderate temperatures.
The heat kills many disease-causing germs and weed seeds.
Mainly heat-loving bacteria and actinomycetes work during this time.
Compost worms move away to cooler edge areas and to the ground.
Very small heaps often do not get properly hot at all.

abschnitte.text: At the start, **mesophilic** microorganisms break down easily degradable substances such as sugars and proteins. Mesophilic means that they like moderate temperatures. Their work produces **metabolic heat**, much as our bodies get warm when we run. This heat builds up in the heap, and the temperature rises day by day. From about 45 to 50 °C the **thermophilic phase** begins.

The word **thermophilic** comes from Greek and means “heat-loving”. In hot composting, mainly thermophilic **bacteria** and **actinomycetes** survive. They break down a lot of material in a short time. Small animals such as woodlice and **compost worms** cannot stand the heat in the core. They retreat to cooler zones at the edge and at the bottom, and only return after it has cooled down.

The high temperatures **sanitise** the compost, which means they make it low in germs. Many plant disease germs and **weed seeds** that could sprout are killed. That is why good compost is so valuable later in the vegetable bed. So that all the material gets hot at some point, experts turn the heap over. That way the cooler edge also ends up inside once.

abschnitte.titel: Not too small, not too hot
abschnitte.text: A very small heap has a lot of **surface** compared with its volume. The heat then escapes faster than it is produced, and hot composting does not happen. But too hot is not good either: well above 70 °C, even useful decomposing organisms die. Breakdown then slows down, and more **nitrogen** is lost as ammonia. Enough air and the right moisture help keep the temperature in the good range.

Depending on the material, the thermophilic phase lasts from a few days to weeks. Afterwards the heap slowly cools down. In the **cooling phase** and the **maturing phase**, fungi, worms and many small animals return. In the end, dark, crumbly soil is produced that smells of forest floor. In Switzerland many municipalities run composting plants in which green waste is put to use in this way.

gewusst: A large compost heap can steam in winter, because it is much warmer inside than the air.
The opposite of thermophilic is psychrophilic, which means cold-loving.

teile.einleitung: Pepper is one of the best-known spices in the world. Black, white and green pepper all come from the same climbing plant from south-western India. In the past, pepper was so valuable that it shaped trade and voyages of discovery.
wichtigste: Pepper originally comes from south-western India.
Black, white and green pepper come from the same plant.
For black pepper, unripe fruits are dried.
For white pepper, ripe fruits have the flesh removed.
The substance piperine makes pepper hot.
In 2022, Vietnam produced the most pepper.

abschnitte.text: The pepper plant is a **climbing plant** that grows several metres up trees or posts. Its home is the **Malabar Coast** in south-western India. It is damp and warm there. The small, round fruits hang in long spikes like tiny bunches of grapes. They are green at first and turn red as they ripen.

All three kinds of pepper come from the same plant and are just processed differently. For **black pepper**, the fruits are harvested unripe and dried. The skin turns dark and wrinkled. For **white pepper**, the fruits are left to ripen and then the flesh is removed, so that only the pale kernel remains. **Green pepper** is harvested unripe and pickled or gently dried so that it stays green.

The heat comes from the substance **piperine**. It irritates certain nerves on the tongue that also react to heat. That is why pepper feels “hot”. Freshly ground pepper smells stronger, because its aromatic substances evaporate during storage. That is why many people only grind it shortly before eating.

In the Middle Ages, pepper was very expensive in Europe, because it came from Asia along long trade routes. Rich merchants were mockingly called **“Pfeffersäcke”**, or pepper sacks. Many seafarers looked for a sea route to India. **Vasco da Gama** was the first European to reach India by sea around Africa, in 1498. Today **Vietnam** is the largest pepper producer, and in 2022 most pepper came from there.

**Pink pepper** is not real pepper. It comes from a quite different plant, the pepper tree from South America, and tastes rather mild and fruity. Chilli or paprika are sometimes also called “pepper”, but they too belong to other plants. Only the fruits of **Piper nigrum** are real pepper.

gewusst: The German saying “Geh hin, wo der Pfeffer wächst”, or “Go where the pepper grows”, used to mean: go as far away as possible, namely all the way to India.
Pepper was so valuable that in the past it was sometimes even used to pay taxes or dues.

teile.einleitung: The lesser celandine is a small early-flowering plant with glossy yellow flowers. It grows in damp, shady places. Its strange German name, “Scharbockskraut”, recalls an old disease of sailors.
wichtigste: The lesser celandine has yellow flowers that shine as if varnished.
Its leaves are rounded to heart-shaped.
Young leaves contain a lot of vitamin C.
“Scharbock” is an old German word for scurvy.
From flowering onwards the leaves become more poisonous.
Small tubers on the roots act as a store.

abschnitte.text: The **lesser celandine** blooms in spring on the woodland floor. Its **yellow** flowers shine strongly, as if they were **varnished**. You can see this especially in the sun. The leaves are rounded to **heart-shaped** and also glossy green. The plant belongs to the **buttercup family**.

The lesser celandine loves **damp** soils and shade. You find it in deciduous woods, by hedges, on stream banks and in parks. Often it forms large green carpets. It blooms early in the year, before the trees have leaves and shade the ground. In early summer the leaves disappear again.

On the roots sit small **tubers**. In them the plant stores **food** for the next year. In this way it can sprout very quickly in spring. New plants can also grow from the tubers. This is how the lesser celandine spreads.

“Scharbock” is an old German word for **scurvy**. In the past, **sailors** often got this disease on long voyages because they lacked fresh fruit and vegetables. The young leaves of the lesser celandine contain a lot of **vitamin C**. That is why they were important in spring in the past. But be careful: from flowering onwards the leaves contain more **poisonous substances**. Then they should no longer be eaten.

gewusst: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
The lesser celandine is one of the first early-flowering plants in deciduous woods.

teile.einleitung: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds still travel far. Animals often help with this. The dispersal of seeds by animals is called **zoochory** in scientific language.
wichtigste: Zoochory is the dispersal of seeds by animals.
In epizoochory, fruits cling to the outside of fur or feathers.
Birds eat berries and pass the seeds out in other places.
Striking red or black berries attract birds.
Ants carry off seeds that have a nutritious attachment, the elaiosome.
Jays and squirrels hide food stores and forget some of them.

abschnitte.titel: Hitching a ride in the fur
abschnitte.text: Some fruits have **hooks** or **barbs**. When a roe deer, a fox or a dog brushes past, they stay caught in the fur. Only later do they drop off, often far away. This kind is called **epizoochory**, where “epi” means on the outside. A well-known example is the **burdock**. The Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral took his inspiration from it for Velcro.

Many plants produce sweet, juicy **berries**. They are often strikingly **red or black**, so that birds can see them easily. The birds eat the flesh of the fruit, and the hard seeds pass through the gut undigested. With the droppings they land in a new place, complete with a little fertiliser. This kind is called **endozoochory**. The **mistletoe** has especially sticky seeds: birds wipe them off on a branch or leave them there, and that way the mistletoe can sprout on a new tree.

In autumn the **jay** hides many acorns in the ground to eat in winter. The **squirrel** buries hazelnuts and beechnuts. Not all hiding places are found again. New trees grow from the forgotten fruits. In the Swiss Alps, the **nutcracker** helps the Swiss stone pine in the same way, by spreading its seeds.

Some seeds carry a small attachment rich in fat and protein, the **elaiosome**. For **ants** it is a delicacy. They carry the seeds into their nest, eat the attachment and then throw the seed away. That way it ends up in a new place. This dispersal is called **myrmecochory**. Examples in our forests are violets and greater celandine.

gewusst: A single jay can hide thousands of acorns in one autumn.
Velcro was invented in Switzerland in the 1950s, modelled on the burdock.

teile.einleitung: Many flowering plants have a built-in recognition system: they notice whether pollen comes from themselves and then do not let it reach fertilisation. This self-incompatibility makes sure that different plants mix.
wichtigste: In self-incompatibility, a plant’s own pollen cannot fertilise.
In this way cross-fertilisation produces more genetic diversity.
It is controlled by a gene locus, the S-locus.
In the nightshade and rose families, the enzyme S-RNase destroys the pollen tube of the plant’s own pollen.
In the cabbage family, the sporophytic form is well researched.
That is why several varieties are planted side by side in apple orchards.
Cowslips show heterostyly, which Charles Darwin studied in detail.

abschnitte.text: When pollen lands on the stigma, a fine **pollen tube** grows from each pollen grain down through the style. Only then can fertilisation take place. In **self-incompatible** plants, the stigma or the style recognises whether the pollen comes from the same plant. If it does, it is stopped. Only foreign pollen reaches its goal.

The recognition is controlled by a particular gene locus, the **S-locus**. In a species there are many variants of it. If pollen and stigma carry the same variant, the pollen is rejected. In the nightshade and rose families, the style makes an enzyme called **S-RNase**. It enters the pollen tube of the plant’s own pollen and destroys it. This form is called **gametophytic**, because the genetic makeup of the individual pollen grain counts.

In the **cabbage family**, to which cabbage and oilseed rape belong, the system works differently and is especially well researched. Here the genetic makeup of the plant that produced the pollen decides. This form is called **sporophytic**. The pollen is usually stopped on the stigma already and cannot even form a tube.

**Apples** too are self-incompatible. An apple tree needs pollen from another, suitable variety for fruit to form. That is why **several varieties** are planted side by side in apple orchards. Bees then carry the pollen from tree to tree. It is similar with many cherries and pears.

Some plants also have different flower forms. In **cowslips** and other primulas there are flowers with a long style and short stamens and ones with a short style and long stamens. This is called **heterostyly**. In this way pollen is exchanged mainly between the two forms. The naturalist **Charles Darwin** studied these flower forms in detail.

gewusst: In some plant species there are dozens of different variants of the S-locus.
The advantage of self-incompatibility is more genetic diversity, which can make plants more resistant to diseases and environmental changes.

teile.einleitung: Some plants move when you touch them. A movement like this in response to touch is called **thigmonasty**. Well-known examples are the sensitive plant and the Venus flytrap.
wichtigste: Thigmonasty is a plant movement triggered by touch.
The direction of the movement does not depend on where the stimulus comes from.
The sensitive plant folds its leaflets together within seconds.
This happens through loss of turgor in small leaf joints.
In the Venus flytrap, the stimulus is passed on by electrical signals.
In the barberry, the stamens snap towards the middle of the flower when touched.

abschnitte.text: The word is put together from Greek: “thigma” means touch. A **nasty** is a movement whose direction is fixed by the structure of the plant. So it does not depend on which side the stimulus comes from. It is different with **thigmotropism**: there the plant grows towards the stimulus, just as the tendrils of a pea wind around a stick. Nasties are often quick, tropisms mostly slow.

The **sensitive plant** comes from tropical America. If you touch it, its leaflets fold together within seconds, and the leaf stalk droops. At the base of the leaves there are **leaf joints**. There, when a stimulus arrives, water flows out of certain cells, the **turgor**, that is the internal pressure, drops, and the leaf folds up. After a few minutes it straightens up again. In experiments, sensitive plants were dropped a short distance again and again without harm: over time they stopped folding their leaves.

The Venus flytrap is a **carnivorous plant**. On its trap leaves there are fine **trigger hairs**. When they are touched, an electrical signal is produced, an **action potential**, similar to the ones in our nerves. After two stimuli in quick succession, the trap snaps shut. If the prey keeps struggling and stimulates the hairs about five times, the plant produces **digestive enzymes**.

The **bladderwort** is a carnivorous water plant that also occurs in Swiss waters. It has small bladders with sensitive hairs. If a tiny animal touches these hairs, the bladder sucks it in in a flash. In the **barberry**, the stamens snap inwards when an insect touches them at the base. That way the insect is dusted with pollen and carries it to the next flower.

gewusst: The trap of the Venus flytrap closes in a fraction of a second.
The suction trap of the bladderwort is among the fastest movements known in the plant kingdom.

teile.einleitung: In a lake the water is not equally warm everywhere. Depending on the season, layers form that do not mix, or all the water is mixed through. This process is called lake circulation.
wichtigste: A dimictic lake mixes completely twice a year.
A polymictic lake is so shallow that it mixes very often.
A meromictic lake has deep water that permanently does not mix.
This sealed-off deep layer is called the monimolimnion.
An amictic lake never mixes, for example because it is permanently frozen over.
In circulation, oxygen reaches the depths and nutrients reach the top.

abschnitte.text: Water has its greatest density at about **4 °C** and is then at its heaviest. In summer the Sun warms the surface. The warm, light water stays at the top, the cold, heavy water at the bottom. Between them lies a **thermocline**, in which the temperature falls rapidly. As long as this layering exists, the water hardly mixes.

In autumn the surface water cools, becomes heavier and sinks. With the help of the wind, the whole lake is finally mixed through. This is called **full circulation**. Many lakes in cool regions mix in this way twice a year, in autumn and in spring. They are called **dimictic**. In winter there is often a layer of ice in between.

Circulation is very important for life in the lake. In it, **oxygen-rich surface water** reaches the depths, where fish and other animals need oxygen. At the same time, dissolved **nutrients** such as phosphate are brought **up from the depths**. There, algae use them for their growth.

abschnitte.titel: Deep lakes such as Lake Geneva
abschnitte.text: Very deep lakes such as **Lake Geneva** do not freeze over. They can mix only in winter. But in **mild winters** the water does not cool enough, and the mixing does not reach the bottom. Then the deep water gets no new oxygen. With climate change this could happen more often.

Shallow lakes that mix completely in almost every storm are called **polymictic**. Lakes whose deep water permanently does not mix with the rest of the water are called **meromictic**. Their sealed-off deep layer is called the **monimolimnion**. Lakes that never mix at all, for example because they are permanently frozen over, are called **amictic**.

gewusst: The north basin of Lake Lugano is regarded as meromictic: its deep water hardly ever mixes with the water above it.
The ending “mictic” comes from the Greek word for “to mix”.

teile.einleitung: A snow bed is a hollow in the mountains where the snow stays especially long. Plants there have only a few weeks to grow. Even so, a very special community of plants lives here.
wichtigste: In a snow bed, snow lies for about nine to ten months of the year.
The wind blows extra snow into the hollow.
The herbaceous willow is regarded as one of the smallest trees in the world.
In the hollows that stay snowy longest, mainly mosses grow.
Alpine snowbells can melt their way through the last of the snow.
In summer the ground stays damp for a long time from the meltwater.

abschnitte.text: A **snow bed** is a hollow or dip in the mountains. The **wind** carries snow from knolls and ridges and deposits it in such sheltered hollows. There the snow cover becomes especially thick. That is why it only melts in **July** or **August**. The snow lies for about **nine to ten months** of the year.

Plants often have only about **two months** without snow cover, in some hollows only a few weeks. This time is enough for only a little growth. That is why the plants there are **tiny** and grow close to the ground. The melting snow soaks the ground. In summer it is therefore usually **damp** and cool.

The **herbaceous willow** is a woody plant whose little stems creep along in the ground. Only a few centimetres with small, round leaves stick up above the earth. It is regarded as one of the **smallest trees in the world**. In the hollows that stay snowy longest, **mosses** often form the main part of the plant cover. They cope well with a very short growing season and a lot of wetness.

The **alpine snowbells** have a special trick. As they sprout, they produce a little warmth through **respiration**. In this way they melt small holes in the thin snow cover. Their delicate, violet, fringed flowers then appear in the middle of the snow. In the Swiss Alps you can watch this in many places in early summer.

gewusst: In high summer a snow bed is often still white while everything around it is already in bloom.
The herbaceous willow also grows in the Arctic.

teile.einleitung: The Black List was in Switzerland a register of non-native plants that harm nature, health or the economy. It helped to identify and combat problem species.
wichtigste: The Black List named invasive neophytes that demonstrably cause damage.
It used to be kept by Info Flora, the national data and information centre for Swiss flora.
Species with possible damage were on the Watch List and were monitored.
Damage to biodiversity, health or the economy was taken into account.
Giant hogweed was on the Black List.
In 2022 it was replaced by lists of the Federal Office for the Environment.
The counterpart for threatened native species is the Red List.

abschnitte.text: **Neophytes** are plants that have come to us through human action only since the discovery of America, either deliberately as ornamental or useful plants or by accident. Most do not cause problems. Some, however, spread strongly and push out native plants. Such species are called **invasive**.

The foundation **Info Flora** used to keep the Black List of invasive neophytes in Switzerland. Species that demonstrably cause damage were put on it. Plants that possibly cause harm were on the **Watch List**. They were monitored so that action could be taken early. In 2022 these lists were replaced by new lists of the **Federal Office for the Environment** (FOEN).

For inclusion in the list, three kinds of damage were considered. First, damage to **biodiversity**, that is, to the variety of native plants and animals. Second, damage to human **health**, for example through allergies or skin injuries. Third, damage to the **economy**, for example to buildings, riverbanks or in agriculture.

**Giant hogweed** can grow several metres tall. Its sap makes the skin sensitive to light, and in sunshine painful blisters form. **Japanese knotweed** grows so vigorously that it can damage riverbanks and walls. **Himalayan balsam** and **Canadian goldenrod** form dense stands and push out other plants. **Ragweed** triggers severe pollen allergies.

abschnitte.titel: The Red List as a counterpart
abschnitte.text: While the Black List warns of harmful non-native species, the **Red List** shows which native species are threatened. In Switzerland there are Red Lists for many groups, for example for plants, birds or butterflies. Both lists help to protect nature in a targeted way.

gewusst: Some invasive plants such as ragweed and giant hogweed are legally banned in Switzerland: you may neither sell nor plant them.
Many invasive neophytes originally come from gardens, from which they escaped into the wild.

teile.einleitung: In the green chloroplasts of plant cells there are tiny, flat membrane sacs: the **thylakoids**. This is where light energy is captured. They are therefore the site of the light reaction of photosynthesis.
wichtigste: Thylakoids are flat membrane sacs in the chloroplast.
The word comes from Greek and means “sac-like”.
Stacked thylakoids form grana that look like rolls of coins.
Stroma thylakoids connect the individual grana with each other.
The inner space of a thylakoid is called the lumen.
Photosystem II is found mainly in the stacked areas.
The most common membrane protein is the light-harvesting complex II.

abschnitte.text: A chloroplast is surrounded by an envelope and filled with a fluid, the **stroma**. The thylakoids lie inside it. Each thylakoid is a flat little sac made of a membrane. Its inner space is called the **lumen**. The name comes from the Greek word for sac and means “sac-like”.

Many thylakoids lie on top of each other like coins in a roll. Such a stack is called a **granum**, and the plural is **grana**. The grana are connected to each other by longer, unstacked **stroma thylakoids**. In this way, all the thylakoids of a chloroplast form a connected network. In the stacked areas sits mainly **photosystem II**, in the unstacked ones rather photosystem I.

In the thylakoid membrane sit **chlorophyll** and many proteins. The **light-harvesting complex II** is the most common membrane protein and acts like an antenna that captures light. The energy drives a chain of reactions in which water is split and oxygen is released. In the process, protons are pumped into the lumen. As they flow back, an enzyme, ATP synthase, makes the energy carrier **ATP**.

abschnitte.titel: Special fats and plants grown in the dark
abschnitte.text: The thylakoid membrane consists for the most part of the lipid **monogalactosyldiacylglycerol**, MGDG for short. This fat with a sugar part is rare in other membranes. When a plant germinates in the dark, finished thylakoids are missing. Instead there is a lattice-like structure, the **prolamellar body**. Only when light arrives do thylakoids form from it, and the seedling turns green.

gewusst: A single leaf contains countless chloroplasts, and each of them has many stacks of thylakoids.
The oxygen we breathe is released from water in the thylakoids.

teile.einleitung: A transplant is a young plant raised in advance that you plant in a bed or in a pot. Many vegetables and flowers are first raised indoors and only later put out in the open.
wichtigste: A transplant is a young plant raised in advance for planting out.
Plants raised in advance have a head start in growth.
Seed pots made of paper or coconut fibre can be planted along with the plant.
Hardening off means slowly getting transplants used to sun, wind and cold.
After planting, you should water the transplant in well.
With too little light, transplants become long and thin.
Carrots and radishes are mostly sown directly in the bed.

abschnitte.text: A **transplant** is a young plant that has been **raised in advance** from a seed in a pot or tray. When it is strong enough, it is put in its final place. You can raise transplants yourself or buy them in spring at the market and in garden centres. Typical are tomatoes, lettuce, cabbage, peppers and many flowers.

Indoors it is already warm in spring, but outside it is still cold. If you raise plants indoors, they get a **head start in growth**. They can then flower and bear fruit earlier. A lot of **light** is important. If a transplant stands too dark, it quickly shoots up, becomes **long and thin** and easily bends over. Gardeners say it is “leggy”.

**Seed pots** made of paper, peat substitute or **coconut fibre** have a great advantage: you can put them in the soil **together with the plant**. In time the pot breaks down in the ground. In this way the fine roots are not injured when transplanting, and the plant takes hold faster.

Plants that have grown indoors know no wind, no strong sun and no cold nights. That is why you have to **harden them off**. For a few days you put them outside at first only for a few hours and then for longer and longer. In this way they slowly get used to the weather. In Switzerland, sensitive transplants such as tomatoes are often planted out only after the **Ice Saints** in mid-May, when there is hardly any more risk of frost.

After planting, you should **water the transplant in well** so that the soil settles around the roots. **Tomato transplants** may even be planted deeper than they stood in the pot. **Additional roots** then form on the stem, and the plant becomes more stable. Some vegetables such as **carrots and radishes**, by contrast, are mostly sown directly in the bed, because they do not tolerate transplanting well.

gewusst: Moving very young seedlings from the seed tray into individual pots is called “pricking out”.
Tomatoes originally come from South America and like it warm, which is why in our climate they are almost always raised as transplants.

teile.einleitung: A sponge city soaks up rainwater like a sponge. Instead of leading the rain into the sewers as fast as possible, it is taken up and stored where it falls.
wichtigste: A sponge city holds rainwater back on the spot and releases it slowly later.
In this way sewers and streams are relieved during heavy rain.
Infiltration swales, green roofs and permeable surfaces are typical building blocks.
Stored water cools the city when it evaporates.
Water that soaks in tops up the groundwater.
China has launched a large state programme for “sponge cities”.

abschnitte.text: In cities many surfaces are **sealed**, that is, covered with asphalt, concrete or roofs. There, rain cannot soak into the ground. In a violent **downpour**, a great deal of water flows into the sewers at the same time. The pipes cannot always swallow it. Then drains overflow, and streets, underpasses and cellars are flooded.

The sponge city turns the principle around: rain should stay as far as possible where it falls. The soil, plants and special stores take up the water and hold it back. Later they release it slowly again, whether into the ground, to plants or to the air. Experts speak of a **near-natural way of handling rainwater**. Swiss cities, too, are increasingly relying on such ideas.

An **infiltration swale** is a shallow, grassed dip. Rainwater collects in it and soaks slowly through the living soil, which filters it as it goes. **Green roofs** store water in soil and plants. In car parks and on paths, permeable surfaces such as **grass pavers** and **permeable paving** help. Vehicles can drive on them, and yet they let water through into the ground.

City trees often have too little room for their roots. In the **Stockholm model**, large pits under streets and squares are filled with coarse **gravel** and soil. Roots can spread in them, and at the same time rainwater is stored. The trees grow healthier and give more shade.

When stored water **evaporates** from the ground and plants, it draws heat from its surroundings. In this way it becomes more pleasant in the city on hot summer days. Water that soaks in instead of running off also tops up the **groundwater**. This is an important source of our drinking water.

gewusst: The idea of the “sponge city” became known worldwide through a large programme in China that was carried out in numerous pilot cities.
A single large tree can evaporate a great deal of water on a hot day and so acts like a natural air conditioner.

teile.einleitung: The sac fungi, also called Ascomycota, are the most species-rich group of fungi. They include yeasts, many moulds, the morel and most lichen-forming fungi. Their name comes from a sac-shaped container for the spores.
wichtigste: Sac fungi form their spores in a sac, the ascus.
A typical ascus contains eight ascospores.
Baker’s yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is a sac fungus.
Many form asexual spores, the conidia.
The common morel is a sac fungus, the chanterelle is not.
Most lichen-forming fungi are sac fungi.

abschnitte.text: Sac fungi form their spores inside a sac-shaped container, the **ascus**. This is where the name **Ascomycota** comes from. When the spores are formed, a **meiosis** takes place first, and then usually a mitosis. In this way **eight ascospores** are formed in a typical ascus. In individual species the number can differ.

Many sac fungi form fruiting bodies in which the asci lie. In the **apothecium** they lie openly on a dish-shaped or cup-shaped surface, for example in the **orange peel fungus**. **Perithecia** are flask-shaped, and **cleistothecia** are completely closed. The **common morel** forms its asci in the honeycomb of its cap. The chanterelle and the parasol mushroom, by contrast, belong to the club fungi.

**Baker’s yeast**, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, is a single-celled sac fungus. It makes bread dough rise and is used for brewing beer. Under favourable conditions it forms asci with usually four spores. Many moulds such as **Penicillium** and **Aspergillus** also belong here. They pinch off **conidia** in large numbers. These are spores that form without the fusion of nuclei and without meiosis.

In 1928, **Alexander Fleming** noticed that a **blue mould** on his bacterial culture inhibited the growth of staphylococci. From this observation came **penicillin**, one of the first antibiotics. Blue moulds belong to the sac fungi. Since then antibiotics have saved a great many lives.

**Lichens** are partnerships of a fungus with algae or cyanobacteria. About 98 per cent of lichen-forming fungi are sac fungi. The fungus forms the body of the lichen and protects its partner. The alga carries out **photosynthesis** and supplies sugar. In the Swiss Alps, lichens cover many rocks.

gewusst: The sought-after truffles also belong to the sac fungi.
Baker’s yeast is among the best-researched living things in the world.

teile.einleitung: Some plants spread their seeds entirely without help from wind, water or animals. They fling them away themselves or simply let them fall. This is called self-dispersal.
wichtigste: The technical term for self-dispersal is autochory.
Touch-me-not is so called because its fruits burst open when touched.
The tension in the capsules comes from water pressure in the cells.
The squirting cucumber squirts its seeds out of the fruit with sap.
In broom, the drying halves of the pod twist and fling the seeds away.
When heavy fruits simply fall to the ground, this is called barochory.
The seeds mostly land near the parent plant.

abschnitte.text: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can travel. Many plants use the wind, water or animals for this. In **self-dispersal**, the plant itself makes sure that the seeds get away. The technical term is **autochory**. The word comes from Greek: “auto” means self, “chorein” means to move on.

Touch-me-not gets its name from the fact that you must not touch it. Its ripe capsules are under tension. If you touch them, they burst open in a flash, curl up and fling the seeds away. The tension comes from **water pressure in the cells** of the capsule wall. Experts speak of **turgor**. The introduced Himalayan balsam spreads especially successfully in this way.

The **squirting cucumber** from the Mediterranean region builds up high pressure in its fruits. When the ripe fruit falls off, it squirts the seeds out together with sap. In **broom**, the pods dry in the sun. The two halves of the pod **twist** as they do so, until they burst open with a crack and fling the seeds away.

The **cranesbill** is named after the long, beak-shaped form of its fruit. As it dries, the parts of the fruit tense and snap upwards, flinging the seeds away. **Barochory** manages entirely without a swing: heavy fruits such as horse chestnuts or acorns simply fall to the ground.

Self-dispersal needs no helpers and works reliably. Its **disadvantage**: the seeds mostly land **near the parent plant**, only a few metres away. With the wind, seeds can travel much further. Often, however, a second dispersal is added, for example when ants carry the seeds away or animals hide acorns.

gewusst: The capsules of touch-me-not open in fractions of a second and are among the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.
If you walk past a broom bush in summer, on warm days you can sometimes hear the cracking of the bursting pods.

teile.einleitung: Sebastian Kneipp was a German priest in the 19th century. He became known because he used cold water for health. His ideas live on to this day in Kneipp facilities, also in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Sebastian Kneipp was a priest and lived in the 19th century.
His cure is associated especially with cold water.
His teaching on health rests on five pillars.
He worked in Bad Wörishofen in the Allgäu.
He described his teaching in the book “My Water Cure”.
Typical of Kneipp facilities is water treading in the stork walk.

abschnitte.text: Sebastian Kneipp was born in **1821** in Swabia in Bavaria and died in **1897**. He came from a poor family of weavers and was determined to become a priest. Later he worked as a **priest** in **Bad Wörishofen** in the Allgäu. There he looked after not only the church but also the sick who came to him.

As a young man, Kneipp fell seriously ill with a lung complaint. By his own account, he read in a book about the healing power of water. He then took **short baths in the cold Danube** in winter. He was convinced that this had cured him. From then on he occupied himself all his life with water treatments.

Kneipp’s teaching rests on **five pillars**. The best known is **water**, for example as affusions, baths or compresses. Added to this are **exercise**, simple, natural **nutrition** and **medicinal plants**, for example as tea. The fifth pillar is a balanced **way of life**, that is, a healthy rhythm of work, rest and sleep.

abschnitte.titel: Water treading in the stork walk
abschnitte.text: In many spa towns, parks and on hiking trails there are **Kneipp facilities**, also in Switzerland. Typical is a basin with cold water. You wade in it in the **stork walk**: with every step you lift one leg completely out of the water. Many people find this refreshing and invigorating. There is often also an **arm bath**, in which you dip your arms into the cold water.

Kneipp wrote down his experiences in the book **“My Water Cure”**. It became a great success and was translated into many languages. Through him Bad Wörishofen became a well-known **spa town**. How strongly individual treatments work is still judged differently today. In the case of illness, the advice of a doctor always belongs with it.

gewusst: In Germany, Kneipp practice is on the list of intangible cultural heritage.
Products such as bath additives and teas are named after Kneipp today.

teile.einleitung: In many lakes the water lies in layers of different temperatures, one on top of another. This is called thermal stratification. It changes with the seasons and is important for the oxygen in the lake and for everything that lives in it.
wichtigste: In summer, warm water lies stably on top of cold water.
The upper layer is called the epilimnion, the deep layer the hypolimnion.
Water is densest at about 4 °C.
Under the ice the colder water lies on top, which is called inverse stratification.
In homothermy the whole lake has the same temperature and can mix.
Because of global warming, summer stratification begins earlier and lasts longer.

abschnitte.text: In summer the sun warms the top layer of water, the **epilimnion**. The **wind** at the surface mixes this layer through, so it usually has an almost uniform temperature. Below it comes the **thermocline**, in which the temperature drops quickly. At the very bottom lies the cold, dense **hypolimnion**. It stays cold all summer and is cut off from exchange with the air.

The phase in which a lake is stably layered in summer is called **summer stagnation**. Warm, light water lies on top of cold, heavy water. The stratification is very stable, even though the difference is only a few degrees. At higher temperatures, the **density** changes more with each degree. That is why the wind needs a great deal of energy to mix the layers.

Water is at its densest at about **4 °C**. That is why water at this temperature sinks downwards. At the bottom of a deep lake that has frozen over, the water in winter is about 4 °C. The colder water close to 0 °C stays directly under the ice. This reversed order is called **inverse stratification**, and it lets fish survive the winter.

In autumn the surface cools down until the whole lake has the same temperature. This state is called **homothermy**. Then there is no difference in density any more, and the wind can turn over the whole lake. As it does so, **oxygen** reaches the depths and nutrients come up to the top. In many lakes this happens in spring and autumn.

**Global warming** also affects Swiss lakes. Warmer surfaces lead to an earlier and more stable summer stratification that lasts longer. This makes mixing in winter harder. As a result, less oxygen reaches the deep water. That can become a problem for fish and other animals in the depths.

gewusst: Because water is heaviest at 4 °C, deep lakes do not freeze through to the bottom.
In very deep lakes it can happen that the water at the bottom does not mix fully with the surface water for years.

teile.einleitung: Terpenes are a huge group of natural substances. They give many plants their scent, for example citrus fruits, conifers or peppermint. Chemically, they are built from units that each have five carbon atoms.
wichtigste: Terpenes are formally built from isoprene units with 5 carbon atoms.
A monoterpene has 10 carbon atoms.
Sesquiterpenes have 15, tetraterpenes 40 carbon atoms.
Beta-carotene is a tetraterpene.
Limonene smells of citrus fruits.
Natural rubber is a polyterpene.
The word terpene comes from turpentine.

abschnitte.text: Terpenes can be described as a chain of several **isoprene units**. An isoprene has the formula C5H8, so **5 carbon atoms**. This is called the **isoprene rule**. Depending on the number of units, different classes are distinguished. Many tens of thousands of different terpenes are known.

A **monoterpene** consists of two isoprene units and has 10 C atoms. **Sesquiterpenes** have 15 C atoms, and “sesqui” means one and a half. Diterpenes have 20 and triterpenes 30 C atoms. **Tetraterpenes** have 40 C atoms, and they include the carotenoids such as **beta-carotene**. **Polyterpenes** consist of very many units, an example being **natural rubber** from the milky sap of the rubber tree.

Many terpenes smell strong. **Limonene** is the main component of the oils in orange and lemon peel. **Menthol** gives peppermint its freshness. **Pinene** gives pine forests their typical scent. Plants use substances like these to ward off animals that eat them or to attract insects.

When **pine resin** is distilled, **turpentine oil** is produced. It consists mainly of monoterpenes such as pinene and is used as a solvent. What is left behind is **rosin**, which is used, for example, to rub on violin bows. The word “terpene” comes from turpentine. Limonene is also used as a fragrance in cleaning products.

The active building block is called **isopentenyl pyrophosphate**. In the cytoplasm it is made from acetyl-CoA by the **mevalonate pathway**. In the plastids there is also the **MEP pathway**. From these C5 building blocks, enzymes put together the many different terpenes. Animals and humans also use the mevalonate pathway, for example for cholesterol.

gewusst: The bluish haze over large forests is partly caused by terpenes that the trees give off into the air.
Rosin from pine resin makes the violin bow grip the strings and set them sounding.

teile.einleitung: A protection forest protects people, houses, roads and railway lines from natural hazards. It holds back avalanches, rockfall and landslides. In Switzerland, about half of the forest has such a task.
wichtigste: About half of the Swiss forest area counts as protection forest.
Trees hold the snow cover in place and prevent avalanches.
Trunks slow down and stop falling stones.
Roots hold the soil together on steep slopes.
Andermatt protected its ban forest as early as 1397 with a ban charter.
A protection forest needs care so that young trees grow up.

abschnitte.text: According to surveys by the Confederation, **about half** of the Swiss forest area counts as **protection forest**. The share is especially large in the **Alpine cantons**. There, villages, roads and railway lines often lie directly beneath steep slopes. Without the forest, many valleys would be far more dangerous. Protection is therefore one of the most important tasks of the forest in Switzerland.

Trunks and crowns break up the **snow cover**. In this way they prevent it from sliding off as a large slab and causing an **avalanche**. In addition, less snow falls directly on the ground. In **rockfall**, a falling stone hits trunks and loses energy. A dense, healthy forest holds back many stones in this way. Above the forest, **supporting structures** of steel or wood are built to hold the snow cover in place.

On steep slopes, the dense **network of roots** anchors the soil like a net. In this way it prevents **landslides** and **erosion**. The forest soil also stores a lot of **rainwater** and releases it slowly. This also helps against flooding in the streams.

Even in the Middle Ages, people knew how important the forest is. In **1397** the valley people of **Andermatt** issued a **ban charter**. In it, use of the forest above the village was forbidden so that it would protect against avalanches. The **ban forest** of Andermatt is well known to this day.

If only trees of the same age grow in a forest, many can collapse at the same time. **Foresters** therefore create gaps in which **young trees** can grow up. Too many **red deer, roe deer and chamois** can endanger the young growth, because they eat buds and shoots. A well-kept protection forest is much **cheaper** than technical protective structures, which are expensive to build and maintain.

gewusst: A protection forest does its work again every year without having to be rebuilt.
The Confederation and the cantons support the care of protection forests with money.

teile.einleitung: In the history of the Earth there have been five great mass extinctions, in which a large share of all species disappeared in a short time. Many researchers are of the opinion that a sixth has begun today, caused mainly by humans.
wichtigste: Before the present one there were five great mass extinctions, the “Big Five”.
A mass extinction is spoken of when about three quarters of species disappear in a geologically short time.
The greatest mass extinction occurred at the end of the Permian.
66 million years ago, an asteroid impact ended the age of the dinosaurs.
Today’s loss of species is caused mainly by humans.
The dodo and the passenger pigeon are well-known examples of extinct birds.

abschnitte.text: Species die out again and again, and this belongs to the development of life. In a **mass extinction**, however, very many species disappear at the same time in a geologically short period. According to the usual definition, it is **about three quarters** of all species. “Short” in the history of the Earth, however, often means thousands or even millions of years.

Experts distinguish **five great mass extinctions**. The first happened about **445 million years ago** at the end of the **Ordovician**. It was linked with an ice age and a falling sea level. Mass extinctions followed in the Devonian and at the end of the **Permian**. This was the greatest: at that time most of all marine species disappeared. After that came the extinction at the end of the Triassic and at the end of the Cretaceous.

The best-known mass extinction happened **66 million years ago**. A large **asteroid** struck the Earth, in the area of today’s Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. Dust and soot darkened the sky, and the climate changed greatly. The dinosaurs died out, except for one group: from it came today’s **birds**. After that the mammals spread.

The **dodo** was a large, flightless bird on the island of **Mauritius**. After the arrival of humans and the animals they brought with them, it died out in the **17th century**. It became a symbol of the loss of species. The **passenger pigeon** was once the commonest species of bird in North America. Through hunting on a massive scale and forest clearance it disappeared. The last passenger pigeon died in **1914** in a zoo.

Today species die out much faster than the natural average. The main causes are the destruction of habitats, overuse, introduced species, pollution and **climate change**. Unlike in the past, then, it is above all **humans** who are the cause. Whether one can already speak of a true mass extinction is debated. In Switzerland, too, the **Red Lists** show that many species are threatened.

gewusst: The journalist Elizabeth Kolbert won the Pulitzer Prize in 2015 for her book “The Sixth Extinction” about today’s loss of species.
The extinction at the end of the Permian is often called “the Great Dying”.

teile.einleitung: Snow is frozen precipitation made up of tiny ice crystals. It forms high up in the clouds and falls to the ground as flakes. In Switzerland, snow shapes the winter, tourism and even our water supply.
wichtigste: Snow is made up of tiny ice crystals.
It forms in clouds when water vapour freezes in the cold.
Fresh snow consists to a large extent of air.
Snow insulates well and protects plants and animals from frost.
In the Alps, snow can set off avalanches.
Melting snow fills rivers and lakes in spring.

abschnitte.text: In clouds there are tiny water droplets and water vapour. When it is colder than zero degrees, the vapour attaches itself to dust particles and forms **ice crystals**. The crystals grow, hook together and become **snowflakes**. When they are heavy enough, they fall, and if it stays cold enough below, they arrive as snow.

In the Alps much more snow falls than on the Central Plateau. On high mountains it stays all year, above the **snow line**, which in the Swiss Alps is usually at around 2,500 to 3,000 metres. **Glaciers** form from old snow that is pressed together over the years. In Davos, the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF studies snow.

Fresh **powder snow** is light and loose and ideal for skiing. Wet snow is heavy and sticky, and good snowmen are built from it. If snow is melted and refrozen several times, grainy **firn** forms. Snowflakes are white because the light is thrown back in all directions by the many crystal faces.

On steep slopes, a layer of snow can slide off and thunder down into the valley as an **avalanche**. In winter the SLF issues an avalanche bulletin every day. It gives the danger level from 1 (low) to 5 (very high). Anyone who goes off the pistes needs training and emergency equipment.

Snow is very important for winter sports and tourism in Switzerland. Where too little falls, snow cannons produce **artificial snow**. In spring the snow melts and feeds streams, rivers and reservoirs for hydroelectric power. Because of climate change, snow lies less often at low altitudes today than it used to.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, regularly shaped piece of frozen water.
Snow that has just fallen.
A large mass of snow that crashes down a slope.
Old, grainy snow that has thawed and frozen several times.

gewusst: Fresh new snow can consist of over 90 per cent air.
Snow squeaks under your shoes in great cold because the crystals break.
A thick blanket of snow keeps the ground beneath it much warmer than the air above.

teile.einleitung: Yarrow is a common meadow flower with white flowers and finely feathered leaves. It smells spicy and has long been used as a medicinal herb.
wichtigste: Yarrow mostly blooms white, sometimes pale pink.
Its leaves are finely divided like little feathers.
Many small flower heads form a flat disc at the top.
When crushed, it smells strongly spicy.
Its Latin name “Achillea” recalls the hero Achilles.
It survives dry weather very well.

abschnitte.text: **Yarrow** mostly blooms **white**, sometimes pale pink. What looks like a flower is a small **flower head** made of many tiny flowers. Many of these heads sit together and form a flat, umbrella-like **disc** at the top. Yarrow belongs to the **daisy family**, like the daisy.

The leaves of yarrow are very finely divided. They look like small green **feathers**. The scientific name is “Achillea millefolium”. “Millefolium” means “thousand leaves”, because each leaf has so many fine lobes. If you crush a leaf, it smells strongly **spicy** and a little bitter, because the plant contains **fragrant oils**.

The German name of yarrow, “Schafgarbe”, contains the word for **sheep**, “Schaf”. It is said that sheep like to eat the plant. The Latin name “Achillea” recalls **Achilles**, a hero from an old Greek legend. According to the legend, he is supposed to have treated wounds with the plant.

**Tea** has been made from yarrow for a very long time. It is said to help with **stomach ache**, for example. Yarrow is very tough. It grows in meadows, on dry **verges** and on banks. It also survives long dry weather well. In Switzerland you find it from the lowlands up into the high mountains.

gewusst: A single flower head of yarrow consists of several tiny individual flowers.
Many insects such as beetles and hoverflies visit the flat flower discs.

teile.einleitung: Teosinte is a wild grass from Mexico and Central America. About 9000 years ago, people bred maize from it. Although the two are closely related, they hardly look alike.
wichtigste: Maize descends from teosinte.
It was domesticated in the south of what is now Mexico.
The closest wild form grows in the Balsas River valley.
Domestication began about 9000 years ago.
Teosinte kernels are enclosed in a hard casing.
An ear of teosinte bears only about 5 to 12 kernels.

abschnitte.text: Genetic studies show that **maize** came from a subspecies of **teosinte**. This subspecies is called Zea mays parviglumis and grows in the valley of the **Río Balsas** in Mexico. Very old traces of maize were found there too. Maize and teosinte are so closely related that they can be crossed. Even so, they look very different.

**Domestication** means that people breed a wild plant over many generations into a crop. With maize this happened in the south of what is now **Mexico**. Genetic dating and finds of starch grains point to a start about **9000 years ago**. Large cobs only appeared over thousands of years. From Mexico, maize spread across the whole of the Americas.

An ear of teosinte consists of only about **5 to 12 kernels** lying one behind the other. A modern maize cob, on the other hand, bears several hundred kernels. Teosinte kernels are enclosed in a **hard fruit casing**. A change in the gene **tga1** exposed the kernel in maize. Another gene, **tb1**, makes sure that maize forms one main stem instead of many side shoots.

For a long time it was unclear where maize came from. The geneticist **George Beadle**, later a Nobel Prize winner, put forward the teosinte hypothesis early on. He studied teosinte and crossed it with maize. Other researchers had other ideas. Only genetic studies confirmed Beadle’s assumption.

gewusst: Teosinte is heavily branched and forms many side shoots, whereas maize mostly has just one strong main stem.
Today maize is one of the most widely grown crops in the world, even though its wild form has only tiny ears.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Park in the Engadine is the only national park in Switzerland. Here nature may develop freely, and humans are only guests. That is why strict rules apply.
wichtigste: Switzerland has a single national park with this strict protection.
It lies in the Engadine in the canton of Graubünden and was founded in 1914.
Visitors must not leave the paths.
Dogs are not allowed in the park, not even on a lead.
Camping is forbidden.
Ibex, marmots and reintroduced bearded vultures live in the park.

abschnitte.titel: The oldest national park in the Alps
abschnitte.text: The Swiss National Park was founded in **1914** and is the oldest national park in the Alps. It lies in the **Lower Engadine** in the canton of **Graubünden**, around the Ofen Pass. The visitor centre is in **Zernez**. The landscape ranges from mountain forests and alpine pastures to rocks and scree. Since the founding, no hunting, felling or mowing has taken place here.

In the national park, nature comes first. That is why you must **not leave the marked paths**. **Dogs** are not allowed at all, because they could disturb wild animals. **Camping**, making fires and sleeping in the open are forbidden. Picking plants, taking stones away or feeding animals is also not allowed. You can stay overnight in a hotel or a hut in the park.

The **ibex** with its large, curved horns was once wiped out in Switzerland. From 1920 it was reintroduced in the national park. Today you often see it on steep slopes. The **marmot** lives in burrows on alpine pastures. If danger threatens, for example from an eagle, it lets out a loud **whistle**, and all disappear into the burrow.

abschnitte.titel: The return of the bearded vulture
abschnitte.text: The **bearded vulture** is one of the largest birds of the Alps. Over a hundred years ago it had disappeared from the Alps. From **1991**, young bearded vultures were released in the national park. Since then bearded vultures breed in Switzerland again. The bearded vulture eats mainly the bones of dead animals, which it sometimes drops from the air onto rocks so that they break.

abschnitte.titel: A laboratory under the open sky
abschnitte.text: Because nature in the park develops without interference, it is very valuable for **research**. Scientists have been observing for decades how forests, meadows and animal populations change. **Red deer**, chamois, foxes and many species of birds also live in the park.

gewusst: The Swiss National Park belongs to the strictest protection category for natural areas of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the IUCN.
The bearded vulture can digest bones so large that it swallows them almost whole.

teile.einleitung: The snowdrop is one of the very first spring flowers. Often it is already blooming while snow still lies. Its white flowers hang downwards like little bells.
wichtigste: The snowdrop has white flowers like little bells.
It mostly blooms in February and March.
It grows from a bulb every year.
The flower has six petals, and the inner ones carry a green spot.
All parts are poisonous, especially the bulb.
Bees find food here as early as February.

abschnitte.text: The **snowdrop** has **white** flowers. They look like little **bells**. Each flower has **six** petals: three long outer ones and three short inner ones. The inner petals carry a **green spot**. The outer ones have no spot.

The snowdrop blooms very early in the year, mostly in **February** and **March**. Often it is still blooming among remnants of snow. That is why it is called snowdrop. The flower **nods downwards**. In this way the pollen stays dry in rain and snow.

In the ground the snowdrop has a small **bulb**. In it, **food** is stored for the next year. That is why it can sprout so early, when it is still cold. In early summer the leaves wither, and the plant rests in the ground until the next winter. In time new bulbs form, and small groups develop.

On warm days, the first **bees** fly out as early as February. They collect **pollen** from snowdrops. For people, however, snowdrops are **poisonous**, all parts and especially the bulb. You may look at them, but not eat them. Ants carry the seeds away and in this way help to spread the plant.

gewusst: Snowdrops can push their way up through thin layers of snow.
In gardens and parks there are often huge carpets of snowdrops.

teile.einleitung: The thermohaline circulation is a gigantic ocean current that links all the world’s oceans with each other. It is driven by differences in the temperature and salt content of the water. It is also called the global conveyor belt of the oceans.
wichtigste: The thermohaline circulation is a worldwide system of ocean currents.
Thermo means heat and haline means salt.
Cold, salty water is heavier and sinks into the depths.
It carries heat and salt water over great distances and influences the climate of whole continents.
The Gulf Stream is also linked to this system and brings warmth to Europe.
One complete circuit takes about 1000 years.
Researchers fear that climate change is weakening the current in the Atlantic.

abschnitte.text: The word **thermohaline** is put together from the Greek words for heat and salt. It describes ocean currents that arise because water is of different weights. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water. Heavy water sinks downwards, lighter water rises, and that is how the sea is set in motion.

In the North Atlantic near Greenland, warm surface water cools down strongly in winter. When **sea ice** forms, the salt stays behind in the water, and the sea water becomes even saltier. This cold, salty water is very heavy and sinks to a depth of several thousand metres. Around Antarctica, too, this kind of **deep water** sinks down.

The water that has sunk flows slowly south along the sea floor and spreads into the Indian and Pacific Oceans. There it gradually rises to the surface again and warms up. As a surface current it finally returns to the Atlantic. This cycle is compared to a **conveyor belt** that takes about 1000 years for one circuit.

abschnitte.titel: The Gulf Stream and Europe’s climate
abschnitte.text: The **Gulf Stream** flows out of the Gulf of Mexico along the coast of North America and across the Atlantic. Its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, brings warm water as far as Norway. That is why it is much milder in Western Europe than in Canada at the same latitude. The weather in Switzerland also benefits from this heat pump of the ocean.

Because of global warming, the ice on Greenland is melting, and a lot of fresh water flows into the North Atlantic. As a result, the sea water there becomes lighter and does not sink as well. Measurements suggest that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or **AMOC** for short, is weakening. A strong slowdown could change the climate in Europe and the rainy seasons in other parts of the world.

The current brings oxygen from the surface into the deep sea, where otherwise hardly any life would be possible. Where nutrient-rich deep water rises again, many fish thrive. The oceans also store a great deal of heat and carbon dioxide. This means the thermohaline circulation plays a key role in the Earth’s **climate system**.

begriffe.erklaerung: How heavy a substance is in relation to its size
How much salt is dissolved in sea water
Cold, heavy water that flows in the depths of the sea
Short for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which includes the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current

gewusst: A drop of water that sinks into the depths near Greenland today will only come back to the surface in about 1000 years.
The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the rivers of the Earth put together.
In the film “The Day After Tomorrow” the current stops within a few days, but in reality it would take much longer.

teile.einleitung: A snow cover is more than just cold whiteness. It acts like a warm blanket for the ground, for plants and for small animals. In the mountains it decides how long the summer lasts for plants.
wichtigste: Fresh powder snow consists of over 90 per cent air.
Under a thick snow cover the ground stays at around 0 degrees.
Without snow, the ground freezes deep in cold winters.
In winter, mice live in the subnivean space under the snow.
The rock ptarmigan digs itself into the snow on cold nights.
If the snow melts early, late frosts can damage young shoots.

abschnitte.text: Fresh **powder snow** consists of over 90 per cent trapped **air**. Air conducts heat badly. That is why snow **insulates** very well. Under a deep snow cover the ground usually stays **at around 0 degrees**, even when it is much colder above. The snow cover holds back the warmth of the ground and shields it from the cold air.

Between the ground and the snow cover lies the **subnivean space**. It is dark there, but steadily cool and windless. **Mice** and other small mammals stay active here all winter. They make **tunnels** and find food. Many plants also spend the winter green under the snow.

The **rock ptarmigan** uses the snow cover as protection. On very cold winter nights it **digs itself into the snow**. In the snow hole it is much warmer than on the surface. In this way it saves valuable energy. In winter its plumage is white, so it is well camouflaged in the snow.

In the mountains there are **hollows** where snow stays especially long. They are called **snow beds**. The snow-free period there often lasts only a few weeks. A plant community of its own grows here, adapted to short summers. Typical is the **herbaceous willow**. It grows only a few centimetres tall and is regarded as one of the smallest trees in the world.

In cold winters with **little snow**, the frost penetrates deep into the ground. This can damage roots and soil organisms. If the snow melts in spring **earlier** than usual, young shoots and buds are directly exposed to **late frosts**. This can seriously damage alpine plants. In Switzerland, the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos studies the snow cover.

gewusst: A snow hole can protect people from cold and wind in an emergency.
No two snow crystals are exactly alike.

teile.einleitung: A savanna is a wide grassland with scattered trees and shrubs. It is found in warm regions of the Earth, and the best known are the savannas of Africa. Many large animals live there.
wichtigste: Mostly grass with scattered trees grows in the savanna.
There is a rainy season and a dry season.
Typical trees are the umbrella thorn acacia and the baobab.
Giraffes, zebras, elephants and ostriches live in the African savanna.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal.
The African elephant is the largest land animal.

abschnitte.text: In the **savanna**, mostly tall **grass** grows. Between it stand scattered trees and shrubs. Savannas are found in Africa, South America, India and Australia. It is warm all year round. A famous area is the **Serengeti** in East Africa.

In the savanna a **rainy season** and a **dry season** alternate. In the rainy season everything turns green and there is plenty of food. In the dry season the grass turns yellow and parched. Many animals then travel long distances to find water and fresh grass.

The **umbrella thorn acacia** has a broad, flat crown like an umbrella. Giraffes like to eat its leaves. The **baobab**, which in German is called the “monkey bread tree”, has a very thick trunk. In it, it stores water for the dry season. In this way both trees survive long months without rain.

With its long neck, the **giraffe** reaches leaves high up in the trees. **Zebras** with their black and white stripes live in **herds**. The **African elephant** is the largest animal that lives on land. The **ostrich** is the largest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it can run very fast.

Predators such as lions, hyenas and cheetahs also live in the savanna. The **cheetah** is the **fastest land animal**. For a short time it can run at over 90 kilometres per hour. But it cannot keep up this speed for long. That is why it first creeps up close to its prey.

gewusst: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern, and no two are exactly alike.
Baobabs can live to be many hundreds of years old.

teile.einleitung: The blackthorn is a thorny shrub found at woodland edges and in hedges. In spring it is full of white flowers, and in autumn it bears blue-black fruits, the sloes.
wichtigste: The fruits of the blackthorn are called sloes.
Ripe sloes are blue-black with a pale bloom.
The blackthorn blooms in March and April, before the leaves.
Sloes are very sour and tart, and after frost they become milder.
The name blackthorn comes from the dark bark and the thorns.
The sloe is a wild plum and is related to the damson.

abschnitte.text: In March and April the **blackthorn** is full of small **white flowers**. The special thing is that it blooms **before the leaves** grow. That is why the whole shrub then looks as if it were covered with snow. The early flowers are an important food for bees and other insects.

The twigs and the bark of the shrub are very **dark**. It also has sharp **thorns**. That is where the name blackthorn comes from. The shrub spreads by **suckers** from the roots. New shoots grow from them, and in time a dense thicket forms.

The small, round fruits are called **sloes**. When ripe they are **blue-black** with a pale, waxy bloom. Picked early in autumn they taste very **sour** and tart and make your mouth pucker. After the first **frost** they become softer and milder. That is why they are often picked late and made into juice, jelly or jam.
